IT : Where assessee builder could not prove expenditure incurred with relevant books and vouchers, estimation of income at rate of 11 per cent was reasonable
Assessment to be made at correct tax rate even if assessee has made excess collection of tax

INCOME TAX : Where during course of assessment proceedings, assessee-builder did not produce books of account and other documents as sought by Assessing Officer, Assessing Officer had rightly rejected books of account of assessee under section 145(3) and estimated income at rate of 10 per cent

IT: Where assessee was unable to produce bills and vouchers relating to purchases, Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in application of GP rate of 15 per cent on declared sales as against 9.27 per cent declared by assessee instead of making addition of whole amount of purchase to cover leakage of profit on account of unverified purchases

INCOME TAX : Where during course of assessment proceedings, assessee did not produce books of account and other documents as sought by Assessing Officer, therefore, Assessing Officer had rightly rejected books of account of assessee under section 145(3) and estimated income at rate of 10 per cent

IT : Where assessee could not substantiate its claim of gross profit rate of 8.7 per cent declared by it as purchase cost and sale price were unverifiable, gross profit rate of 11 per cent determined by Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal was justified

IT : Where in course of appellate proceeding Tribunal concluded that in block assessment proceedings only 15 per cent of total sales receipts be taken for purpose of levy of tax, in view of sub-section (2) of section 158B, impugned direction of Tribunal did not require any interference

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in business of freight transport by road, failed to substantiate genuineness of expenditure incurred, however incurrence of expenditure could not be doubted while achieving a high volume of turnover, profit of assessee was to be estimated at 10 per cent of gross receipts

INCOME TAX : Where a notice under section 148 was issued for re-opening of assessments on ground that GP Rate at rate of 12.5 per cent should have been levied instead of 8 per cent on estimated unrecorded sales, since there was no allegation that assessee suppressed income or did not disclose income from unrecorded sales, impugned reopening notice issued against assessee was to be set aside

IT : When physical verification of stocks was carried out during regular assessment, revision to value stock on basis of last year G.P. of 10 per cent as against books which were accepted by Assessing officer could not be accepted
IT/ILT: Since RPT percentage of 15-20 per cent was confirmed by various Tribunals, RPT of comparable being 18.3 per cent, it need not be excluded from comparable list

status of the hotel. Reasonable and fair estimate has to be arrived at. In the instant case, hotel was located at Bhatinda and the furnishing of the hotel could reasonably be estimated. So far as applicability of section 10(14 ) was concerned, from the assessment year 1988-89, approval from the Government of India was not available to the assessee on the allowances. Therefore, the assessee was not entitled for the benefit under section 10(14 ). With regard to levy of interest under section 234B, section 234B, sub-section (1), Explanation (1) defines ‘assessed tax’. According to Explanation (1), for the purpose of calculating interest, tax on the assessed income as assessed under section 143(1) or 143(3) is to be reduced by tax deducted or collected at source on any income which is subject to such deduction. The tax deducted or collected is to be interpreted for the purpose of section 234B. The important interpretation relates to the fact whether or not the assessee is liable to advance tax. For working out liability of advance tax, one has to look into section 210 and section 210 comes into operation if section 209 becomes applicable on the income of the assessee. Thus, for making the assessee liable to advance tax and while making estimate, he shall reduce the amount of income-tax which would be deductible or collectible at source. Section 209(1)(d) is clear on the given situation. The Explanation of the provision in simple language is whether or not the person who has to deduct tax at source makes deduction. The assessee has to reduce the tax deduction at source which is deductible from the estimate of his income and estimate of his tax. Under those circumstances, the impact of section 234B, Explanation (1) will be that such amount will logically be reduced from the assessed tax because in section 234B, there has to be a finding that advance tax is payable as envisaged under section 210. In the instant case, even tax deducted at source from the salary was, in fact, deducted. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified in recording the finding that the assessee was liable to make payment under section 234B.

In the result, the appeal was partly allowed.

under section 7 and within upper limit fixed by such standard rent, rent which owner may reasonably expect to get, if premises are let out as a single unit to a hypothetical tenant, would be the rateable value - Held, yes - Whether where addition made is of a distinct and separate unit of occupation, rateable value of premises would have to be determined on basis of formula laid down for assessing rateable value of premises which are partly self-occupied and partly tenanted - Held, yes. FACT: The petitioners filed writs in the High Court, challenging the assessment made by the Municipal Corporation determining the rateable value of certain categories of properties situate in Delhi. These writs, which were later transferred to the Supreme Court, related to four different categories of properties, namely, (i) where the properties were self-occupied, (ii) where the properties were partly self-occupied and partly tenanted, (iii) where the land on which the property was constructed was leasehold land with a restriction that the leasehold interest should not be transferred without the approval of the lessor, and (iv) where the property had been constructed in stages.

HELD: So far as properties situated in the union territory of Delhi except New Delhi are concerned, the determination of a rateable value for the purpose of assessability to property tax is governed by the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, while the determination of rateable value for the purpose of assessability to property tax in respect of properties situated in New Delhi is governed by the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911. The relevant provisions of both these statutes in respect of determination of rateable value for the purpose of assessability to property tax are almost identical.

Thus, the principles governing determination of rateable value under the provisions of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, would apply equally in relation to determination of rateable value under the provisions of the Punjab Municipal Act.

Under the provisions of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, the criteria for determining rateable value of a building is the annual rent at which such building might reasonably be expected to be let from year to year, less certain deductions which are not material for the purpose of these petitions. The word 'reasonably' in this definition is very important. What the owner might reasonably expect to get from a hypothetical tenant, if the building were let from year to year, affords the statutory yardstick for determining the rateable value. Now, what is reasonable, is a question of facts and it depends on the facts and circumstances of a given situation. The process of reasoning, which would be followed in fixing reasonable rent, would be first to ascertain what is standard rent payable in case of similiar or nearly similar premises in the locality, and then to consider how far such standard rent in its application to the premises, needs adjustment having regard to the situation, locality and condition of the premises and the amenities provided therein. The reasonable rent so determined would be the standard rent of the premises. There may, however, be cases where there are no similar or nearly similar premises in the locality and in such cases, guideline to the Controller would not be available and the Controller would have to determine as best as he can, what rent would be reasonable having regard to the situation, locality and condition of the premises and the amenities provided therein. But such cases would, by their very nature, be extremely rare and even there the Controller would not be on an uncharted sea : he would have to fix the reasonable rent of the premises taking into account the standard rent of similar or nearly similar premises in the adjoining locality and making necessary adjustments in such standard rent. The rateable value of a building cannot exceed the measure of standard rent, whether determined by the Controller under section 9 of the Rent Act or arrived at by the assessing authority by applying the principles laid down in the Rent Act, but it may, in a given case, be less than the standard rent having regard to various attendant circumstances and considerations.

In the case of self-occupied residential premises, the rateable value of the premises would be the annual rent at which the premises might reasonably be expected to be let to a hypothetical tenant and such reasonable expectation cannot, in any event, exceed the standard rent of the premises, though in a given situation, it may be less than the standard rent. The standard rent would constitute the upper limit of the annual rent which the owner might reasonably expect to get from a hypothetical tenant, if he were to let out the premises. Obviously, in such an eventuality, the standard rent would be determinable on the principles set out in sub-section (1)(A)(2)(b) of section 6 of the Rent Act.

HEADNOTE: Section 143, read with section 256, of Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 33, read with section 66, of Indian Income tax Act, 1922] - Assessment - General - Assessment year 1924-25 - In respect of contracts spread over a number of years, assessee produced accounts but accounts for relevant accounting year could not be separated - ITO assessed profit at a standard rate without informing assessee of information or evidence on which rate was based and without giving him any opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal - Whether question of law arose out of order of ITO - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee, a contractor, was assessed to income-tax for the relevant assessment year in respect of certain contracts which commenced in 1922 and were finished some time in 1924. The assessee produced his accounts, but the accounts for the relevant accounting year could not be separated. The ITO considered the accounts to be unreliable. He, therefore, assumed profit at the standard rate of 10 per cent for the purposes of his assessment. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner concluded that in any case it was impossible to ascertain from the assessee’s accounts what the income had been for one year and, therefore, the only way of ascertaining it was to apply the usual rate of 10 per cent on the total payments received. On application under section 66(2) of the 1922 Act, the Commissioner declined to make any reference.

On application under section 66 (3) of the 1922 Act.

HELD: In the instant case the assessee did not allege that he derived no income at all from any contracts, nor did the assessment proceed definitely on the ground that the accounts were unreliable. The Assistant Commissioner adopted a standard rate for the assessment merely because no separate accounts were available for the accounting year. This was apparently due to the manner in which the accounting were kept. As the assessee failed to produce correct and complete accounts for the accounting year, it was open to the Income-tax Officer to make an assessment to the best of his judgment: vide section 23, read with section 11, of the 1922 Act. The Assistant Commissioner, however, gave no reasons for adopting what he called the usual rate of 10 per cent for the purposes of the assessment, and it was not known how that rate was arrived at. In the circumstances of the case, the point of law emerged for decision was whether in the case of a contract spread over a number of years when accounts for the year under assessment could not be separated, the ITO was legally justified in assessing profits at a flat rate without informing the assessee of the information or evidence on which the rate was based and without giving him any opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal.

Accordingly, the petition was accepted and the Commissioner was directed to state the case and refer the point of law to the High Court for decision.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Sardha Ram for the Assessee .

CIT [1996] 218 ITR 612,  assessment having been completed after issuance of notice under section 148, was not a regular assessment and, therefore, interest under section 139(8) was not chargeable - Held, yes

Section 234A/234B/234C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Advance tax - Interest for defaults in furnishing return/payment of - Assessment year 1989-90 - Whether in view of fact that law had with effect from 1-4-1989, decision in Shakti Tiles’ case, delivered with reference to section 139(8)/217 in assessee’s case for preceding assessment year, was not applicable and, therefore, interest under sections 234A, 234B & 234C was rightly charged even though assessment was completed after notice under section148 - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 1988-89, the assessee contended that the assessment having been completed after issuance of notice under section 148, was not a regular assessment, and so interest under sections 217 and 139(8) could not be charged. For the assessment year 1989-90, on the same lines the assessee challenged charging of interest under sections 234A, 234B and 234C.

On second appeal:

HELD: The Madhya Pradesh High Court in the case of Shakti Tiles Industries v. CIT [1996] 218 ITR 612, held that the assessment made after issuance of notice under section 148 was not either under section 143 or section 144 and since the return was filed beyond the prescribed period, there was no return in the eye of law, and that it being not a case of regular assessment, interest under section 139(8) was not leviable. Therefore, following the aforesaid decision in the instant case, interest charged under section 139(8)/217 was cancelled.

However, for the assessment year 1989-90, the law had changed and as per section 234A, Explanation 3, an assessment which was made for the first time under section 147, shall be regarded as regular assessment. Similar is an Explanation 2 to section 234A, while in the section 234C, there is no reference to the regular assessment. In view thereof, the above decision delivered with reference to section 139(8)/217 would not be applicable in respect of charging of interest under sections 234A, 234B and 234C. Hence, the validity of charging of interest under sections 234A, 234B and 234C was upheld.

a) or (2)(b) or (1)(A)(2)(b) or (1)(B)(2)(b) of section 6, as may be applicable and keeping in mind the upper limit fixed by the standard rent and taking into account the various factors, the assessing authorities would have to determine the rent which the owner of the premises may reasonably expect to get if the premises are let out to a hypothetical tenant and such rent would represent the rateable value of the premises. When any addition is made to the premises at a subsequent stage, three different situations may arise. Firstly, the addition may not be of a distinct and separate unit of occupation but may be merely by way of extension of the existing premises which are self-occupied. In such a case, the original premises together with the additional structure would have to be treated as a single unit for the purpose of assessment and its rateable value would have to be determined on the basis of the rent which the owner may reasonably expect to get, if the premises as a whole are let out subject to the upper limit of the standard rent determinable under the provisions of section 6(1)(A)(2)(b). Secondly, the existing premises before the addition might be tenanted and the addition might be to the tenanted premises, so that the additional structure also forms part of the same tenancy. Where such is the case, the standard rent would be liable to increase under section 7 and such increased rent would be the standard rent of the premises as a whole and within the upper limit fixed by such standard rent, the assessing authorities would have to determine the rent which the owner may reasonably expect to get if the premises as a whole are let out as a single unit to a hypothetical tenant and in such a case, the actual rent received would be a fair measure of the rent which the owner may reasonably except to receive from such hypothetical tenant unless it is influenced by extra-commercial considerations. Lastly, the addition may be of a distinct and separate unit of occupation and in such a case, the rateable value of the premises would have to be determined on the basis of the formula laid down for assessing the rateable value of premises which are partly self-occupied and partly tenanted. The same principles for determining of rateable value would obviously apply in case of subsequent additions to the existing premises. The basic point to be noted in all these cases is that the formula set out in sub-sections (1)(A)(2)(b) and (1)(B)(2)(b) of section 6, cannot be applied for determining the standard rent of an addition, as if that addition was the only structure standing on the land. The assessing authorities cannot determine the standard rent of the additional structure by taking the reasonable cost of construction of the additional structure and adding to it the market price of the land and applying the statutory percentage of seven and a half to the aggregate amount. The market price of the land cannot be added twice over, once while determining the standard rent of the original structure and again while determining the standard rent of the additional structure. Once the addition is made, the formula set out in section 6(1)(B)(2)(b) can be applied only in relation to the premises as a whole and where the additional structure consists of a distinct and separate unit of occupation, the standard rent would have to be apportioned in the manner indicated above.

In the petitioners case also, the rateable value of different categories of properties was liable to be assessed under the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act and under the Punjab Municipal Act in accordance with the principles outlined above.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Valuation of stock - Assessment year 1959-60 - While completing assessment ITO did not accept assessee's reasons for low profits at rate of 9% in respect of a contract undertaken by him and applied flat rate of 12Â½% profit - On appeal assessee had not derived before AAC that full quantitative details were not available in respect of stores of value of Rs. 1,30,000 - For subsequent assessment year assessee declared a profit of 9.9% - Whether on facts provisions of section 13 were applicable to assessee's case and therefore, Tribunal was justified in upholding addition in assessee's income - Held, yes

FACT: The business of the assessee was execution of construction contracts. The assessee commenced its business from 25-1-1958, and the accounts were closed for the first time on 25-1-1959. During the accounting year the assessee undertook three contracts with respect to which it submitted separate profit and loss statements.

The accounts in respect of the first two contracts were accepted by the authorities under the Act in toto but with regard to the accounts relating to the third contract the ITO declined to accept the assessee's reasons for low profits at the rate of 9% in respect of that contract. He, therefore, applied a flat rate of 12Â½% profit and made certain addition to the assessee's income.

On appeal, the AAC had accepted the assessee's reasons for the low profit of 9% but had sustained an addition of Rs. 10,000 on the ground that the assessee's representative had not denied before him that full quantitative details might not be available in respect of the stores of the value of over Rs. 1,30,000 consumed in the execution of the contract. When the case came up before the Tribunal the addition of Rs. 10,000 was found to be excessive and was reduced to Rs. 6,000.

On reference :

HELD: In the instant case there was material before the Tribunal on which its finding could be based: the assessee's representative had admitted before the AAC that full quantitative details in respect of the stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 consumed in the execution of that contract might not be available. In the circumstances, recourse to estimating the profits on the contract was inevitable. He, therefore, made an addition of Rs. 10,000 as against Rs. 26,434 added by the ITO. If the assessee wished to displace the AAC's estimate it was open to him to adduce evidence in support of its claim that the consumption of stores of the value of Rs. 1,30,000 was fully justified. This the assessee apparently did not do. For the subsequent year 1960-61 the assessee itself declared a net profit rate of 9.9% as against 9% declared in the assessment year in question. It could not be disputed that this was additional material which the Tribunal could take into consideration as it did. There was thus material before the Tribunal on which its estimate was based. The Tribunal's decision was, therefore, in conformity with the decision in the case of CIT v. Maharajadhiraj of Darbhanga [1933] 1 ITR 94 (P.C.).

The Tribunal was therefore justified in holding that the proviso to section 13 was applicable and there was material before it to sustain the aforesaid addition.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of revenue.

clear that the question referred in the instant case was decided by the Division Bench in the case of Ranchi Club Ltd. (supra) and the said judgment was affirmed by the Supreme Court (See Annex). It may be noted that the Supreme Court, after hearing the parties, dismissed the appeal. Therefore, it was not a case where special leave petition was summarily dismissed by the Supreme Court, rather civil appeal was heard on merit and thereafter it was dismissed holding that the appeal had no merit. It is well-settled principle of law that when a special leave petition is summarily dismissed under article 136 of the Constitution, such dismissal does not lay down any law; rather it shall be deemed that the Supreme Court has simply held that it is not a fit case where special leave petition should be granted. The same principle will not apply in a case where civil appeal is dismissed by the Supreme Court holding that the appeal has no merit. When once civil appeal is dismissed after hearing the parties by the Supreme Court holding that the appeal has no merit, then such order becomes one which attracts article 141 of the Constitution, which provides that the law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all the Courts within the territory of India.

Having regard to the law laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of V.M. Salgaocar & Bros. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2000] 243 ITR 383/110 Taxman 67, the questions referred to the Full Bench had been completely answered by the Division Bench of the High Court in the assessee's case, and the same had been affirmed in civil appeal by the Supreme Court. Hence, there was no question of going any further and taking a different view in the matter.

Further from examining the various provisions, it is manifest that assessment made under section 143 includes reassessment as well. An assessment made in pursuance of a notice under section 148 is a regular assessment under section 143 or section 144. Section 140A provides that any admitted tax paid in pursuance of this section shall be deemed to have been paid towards a regular assessment under section 143 or 144. Accordingly, any assessment made for the first time by resort to section 147 would also be a regular assessment for the purpose of section 143.

From reading of provisions of sections 234A and 234B along with Explanation, it is clear that tax on the total income as determined under section 143(1) or on regular assessment shall be deemed to be tax on total income as declared in the return for the purpose of computing the interest payable under section 140A. Also, the additional liability to pay interest arises only on account of delayed filing of return or non-filing of return and also on account of delayed or non-payment of advance tax. According to the CBDT Circular No. 549, dated 31-10-1989, if the returned income is increased either as a result of adjustment made under the first proviso to section 143(1)(a) or as a result of regular assessment under section 143(3) so that the advance tax paid becomes less than 90 per cent of the tax on the total income determined under section 143(1)(a) or on a regular assessment, interest under section 234A will also be increased on the basis of the tax on total income determined under section 143(1)(c) or on regular assessment.

Explanation 4 to section 234A fully clarifies the position by explaining that tax on the total income as determined under sub-section (1) of section 143 or on regular assessment shall be deemed to be the tax on total income as declared in the return for the purpose of computing the interest payable under section 140A.

Thus, it was to be held that (i) the decision rendered by Division Bench in Ranchi Club Ltd.'s case (supra), which has been affirmed by the Supreme Court in civil appeal in [2001] 114 Taxman 414 (SC), had correctly decided the issues which were the subject-matter of this reference; (ii) that interest under sections 234A and 234B is leviable on the tax on the total income as declared in the return and not on the income as assessed and determined by the assessing authority; and (iii) that in absence of any specific order of the assessing authority, interest could not be charged and recovered from the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits Assessment year 1964-65 - Assessee was a military contractor - Finding some irregularities in accounts, ITO assessed profits of assessee from military contracts by applying flat rate of 10 per cent on total receipts - Tribunal held that price of stores supplied by Government was to be excluded while applying flat rate to assessee's contract receipts - Whether order passed by Tribunal was justified - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a military contractor. During the relevant accounting period, the assessee took three military engineering service contracts. The ITO found that the expenditure of the assessee was not supported by vouchers and he detected some other mistakes also in the accounts. After applying the provisions of section 145(1), the ITO assessed the profit from these contracts by applying a flat rate of 10 per cent on the total receipts. The AAC allowed the appeal of the assessee and held that no rate of profit could be applied on the value of the stores supplied by the Government and this order was upheld by the Tribunal.

On reference, the Division Bench noticed the divergent views taken by the various High Courts and particularly because of the challenge laid to the correctness of the judgment in Brij Bhushan Lal v. CIT [1971] 81 ITR 497 (Punj.) and, thus, referred the matter for decision of the Full Bench.

HELD: The Supreme Court in Brij Bhushan Lal Parduman Kumar v. CIT [1978] 115 ITR 524 (SC) reversed the said judgment of the High Court (supra) and held that the assessment was to be made excluding the cost of material and stores received for being used in the works undertaken by the contractor. Following, the aforesaid decision, it was to be held in the instant case that the Tribunal was justified in holding that price of stores supplied by Government was not to be included while applying the flat rate to the assessee's contract receipts.

Note : The decision was in favour of assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 145, read with sections 4 and 256 of Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13, read with sections 3 and 66 of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Estimation of profits - Assessment years 1936-37 to 1938-39 - Whether proviso to section 13 of 1922 Act is very wide in its scope and no point of law arises where flat rate is applied with sufficient reason given - Held, yes - Whether where directing himself by decisions of Privy Council and taking into consideration all facts of case, including previous conduct of assessee Commissioner came to conclusion that there was no nucleus from which the property could have been acquired, that there was no evidence that it had been thrown into common stock, and that income from this property was his individual income, no referable question of law arose - Held, yes

Whether 37(1), read with section 256 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2), read with section 66 of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment years 1936-37 to 1938 - Whether question whether expenditure upon leases was capital expenditure or expenditure incurred solely for purposes of business was a referable question of law - Held, yes - Whether there being no authorities by Oudh Chief Court on that point, merely because it was probable that Oudh Chief Court would follow previous decisions of other High Courts was not sufficient reason for refusing to direct Commissioner to state case - Held, yes

FACT: While completing the assessment for the assessment years 1936-37 to 1938-39, the Department under section 13, applied the rate of 20 per cent in respect of profits from the Military department contracts and 15 per cent in respect of the other two, because it was not possible from the accounts to work out what the actual net profits were. The department further held that the applicant was to be assessed as an individual and not as a Hindu joint family. The Commissioner also held that the expenditure upon the leases should be treated as capital expenditure and refused to state a case under section 66(2).

On an application under section 66(3):

HELD: Directing himself by the decisions of the Privy Council and taking into consideration all the facts of the case, including the previous conduct of the present applicant, the Commissioner came to the conclusion that there was no nucleus from which the property could have been acquired, that there was no evidence that it had been thrown into the common stock, and that the income from this property was his individual income. Therefore, the Commissioner was right in holding that no question of law arose.

As regards the application of that rate of profit, the Commissioner had given reasons for not being able to discover what the yearly income was and these seemed to be sufficient. Section 13, proviso, is very wide in its scope and no point of law arises where flat rate is applied with sufficient reason given. In respect of the expenditure , it was argued that the expenditure upon the leases should not have been regarded as a capital expenditure but as "expenditure incurred solely for the purposes of earning profits" which coul d be deducted from the income. There was undoubtedly a point of law involved here, the decision of which was not on the face of it very easy. There were authorities on the point but none of the Chief Court. The fact that it seems probable that the Chief Court would follow previous decisions of other High Courts was not, sufficient reason for refusing to direct the Commissioner to state the case.

The Commissioner was, therefore, directed to state a case for opinion of High Court on the point as to whether the amount of Rs. 1,436 was capital expenditure or was an expenditure incurred solely for the purposes of the business.

Note : The case was decided partly in favour of the assessee and partly in favour of revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 160 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 41(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Trust Trustees - Assessment of - Assessment years 1959-60 to 1961-62 - Pursuant to directions of AAC income of Wakf was excluded from assessee's individual income - Separate assessments were made by ITO and notices of demand were issued to assessee - Though tax was levied at maximum rate but no reference to section 41(1) of 1922 Act was made and, it was not stated that shares of beneficiaries were not determinate - Whether statutes did not impose upon ITO a duty to set out reasons or to quote section under which power of making assessment was exercised - Held, yes - Whether computation of tax was sufficient determination by ITO as required by Act and failure or omission to quote section of Act under which assessment was made or to set out reasons for making assessment at maximum rate could not be treated as an error of law apparent on face of records, justifying interference by High Court by issue of writs or orders under article 226 of the constitution - Held, yes

FACT: Besides the properties, which were dedicated as wakf, and of which the assessee was the mutwalli, he was the owner of certain other properties. Under the deed of wakf, the assessee and his sons and daughters were the beneficiaries. The person who dedicated the properties dies on 19-1-1937. The gross income of the wakf estate was alleged to be Rs. 34,000 per year. For the assessment years 1958-59 to 1960-61, the income derived from the personal properties of the assessee was lumped together with the income from the wakf estate, and the assessee was assessed as an individual on the aggregate income.

On appeal, the AAC directed that the assessee should be taxed separately in respect of the income from the said wakf estate and such income should be excluded from the assessee's individual assessments. Pursuant to this direction separate assessments were made under section 23(3), of 1922 Act, for the income arising from the wakf estate and notices of demand for the years 1958-59 to 1961-62 had been issued to the assessee. For the assessment year 1958-59, the income from the wakf estate was assessed, in the status of an association of persons. The tax was computed at the maximum rate under the first proviso to section 41(1) of 1922 act on the ground that the shares of the beneficiaries under the Wakf were not determinates. Assessee's appeal before the AAC was pending.

For the assessment years 1959-60 to 1961-62 also the tax was computed at the maximum rate. But while, for the assessment year 1958-59, it was stated in the assessment order that it was made under section 23(3) and section 41(1) of 1922 Act in the assessment orders for the years 1959-60 to 1961-62 where was no reference to section 41(1) of 1922 Act. But it was mentioned that the assessments were made under section 23(3) of 1922 Act and the tax was again levied at the maximum rate. The assessee felt aggrieved by the computation of the tax at the maximum rate for the said three assessment years, and instead of preferring an appeal, he moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution and obtained a rule nisi. This rule was discharged by a judgment dated 7-7-1964.

On appeal, it was contended on behalf of assessee that as there was nothing in the orders to show that they were made under section 41(1) of 1922 Act, and as there was no finding that the beneficiaries were an indeterminate class of persons, the tax could not be computed at the maximum rate and, therefore, there was an error of law apparent on the face of the records. On the other hand, it was contended for the Department that the computation of tax was sufficient determination by the ITO as required by the Act and failure or omission, to quote the section of the Act under which the assessment was made or to set out the reasons for making the assessment at the maximum rate could not be treated as error of law apparent on the face of the records, justifying interference by the High Court by issue of writs or orders under article 226 of the Constitution.

HEADNOTE: Section 44AC, read with section 206C, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Alcoholic liquor/timber trade - Special provision for computing profits and gains from - Assessment year 1992-93 - In his order under section 263 Commissioner held that assessment completed under section 143(1)(a) without invoking provisions of section 44AC was erroneous insofar as it was prejudicial to interests of revenue and, accordingly, directed Assessing Officer to modify assessment - Whether, in view of decision of Supreme Court in Union of India v. A. Sanyasi Rao [1996] 219 ITR 330/85 Taxman 321, Commissioner was justified in directing Assessing Officer to modify assessment and to recompute taxable income in light of section 44AC read with sections 28 to 43C - Held, yes

Section 143 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Assessment - Whether assessment made under section 143(1)(a) can be called a regular assessment - Held, no

FACT: Assessment for the assessment year 1992-93 had been made under section 143(1)(a) at returned income. The Commissioner found that the assessment was made without invoking section 44AC. He, therefore, held that the assessment order was erroneous, insofar as it was prejudicial to the interests of the revenue, and issued show-cause notice under section 263. The Commissioner rejected the assessee’s contention that there was no error in the assessment order in view of the decision of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in A. Sanyasi Rao v. Government of Andhra Pradesh [1989] 178 ITR 31/ 43 Taxman 271 and the decision of the Supreme Court in A. Sanyasi Rao’s case (supra), and directed the Assessing Officer to modify the assessment order and re-compute the taxable income of the assessee in the light of section 44AC read with sections 28 to 43C.

On appeal :

HELD: In view of the decision of the Supreme Court in A. Sanyasi Rao’s case (supra), it was to be held in the instant case that the Commissioner was justified in directing the Assessing Officer to re-compute the taxable income of the assessee in the light of the provisions of section 44AC read with sections 28 to 43C, as the assessment made under section 143(1)(a ) cannot be called a regular assessment in view of the expression ‘regular assessment’ defined in section 2(40) as amended by the Finance Act, 1990 with effect from 1-4-1989. In view of the said definition, ‘regular assessment’ means assessment made under section 143(3) or section 144. In this connection, reference may also be made to the Explanation inserted under section 143 by the Finance (No.2) Act, 1991 with effect from 1-10-1991, which provides that an intimation sent to the assessee under section 143(1) or 143(1B) shall be deemed to be an order for the purpose of sections 246 and 254. However, the intention of the said Explanation was only to provide for appeal against an order made under section 143(1)(a). Thus, the order of the Commissioner was to be confirmed.

appeal, the Deputy Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessment orders. Feeling aggrived, the assessee filed revisions under section 264 before the Commissioner who dismissed the same.

On writ, the assessee contended that the ITO had not discussed as to on what basis he arrived at the total figure of sales and the net profit rate of 9 per cent; and, thus, in the absence of any material on record, the order passed by the authorities deserved to be quashed. HELD: In view of catena of decisions, the assessee’s challenge to the total estimated sales taken by the Assessing Officer was not sustainable The said estimated sales taken by the Assessing Officer was based on the information furnished by the assessee himself on Form No. 45D under section 133B. It could also not be challenged in the instant petition as it was not challenged by the assessee in revision filed before the Commissioner. The contention of the assessee that the rate of tax had been fixed arbitrarily at 9 per cent, per annum had force. The assessee submitted copy of trading and profit and loss account for both the assessment years before the first appellate authority (Deputy Commissioner (Appeals)). It was stated that the said trading and profit and loss account were prepared by him on the basis of the books of account maintained by him and were checked and inspected by the authorities, during the survey conducted under section 133B. It was also contended before the appellate authority that on the basis of the accounts maintained by him, his income did not exceed taxable quantum for both the years. However, no attention was given to the assessee’s contentions by the Deputy Commissioner (Appeals) though the Deputy Commissioner (Appeals) on the basis of the said trading and profit and loss account accepted the sales shown by the assessee. However, he maintained the rate of 9 per cent, by observing that it was reasonable for the medicine shop business. That reasoning appeared to be arbitrary and unreasonable in view of the Division Bench judgment of the Madhya Pradesh High Court in the case of Ganga Prasad Sharma v. CIT [1981] 132 ITR 87 . The appellate authority ought to have assigned some reason as to why the accounts submitted by the assessee could not be considered for arriving at the figure of rate of tax. The said judgment makes it clear that the power to pass assessment order on the basis of best judgment is not an arbitrary power. It must be based on some relevant material. It must be fair and reasonable. The assessment of rate by merely observing that generally computation of profit of 9 per cent was reasonable in medicine shop business was arbitrary and was not sustainable. The appellate authority had not disclosed as to why it had not taken into consideration the trading and profit and loss account submitted by the assessee and on what basis the computation was made. On the other hand, as reflected from the order, the basis of computation of profit at 9 per cent was general and casual. The revisional authority also rejected the assessee’s prayer to reduce the net profit rate without assigning any reasons as to how the rate of 9 per cent was just and reasonable.

Therefore, the orders passed by the appellate authority and the revisional authority were to be held to be arbitrary to the extent that they upheld the rate of 9 per cent and were, therefore, to be quashed. The matter was to be remitted to the appellate authority to be reconsidered as to the rate which could be applied while estimating net profits.

Accordingly, the petition was to be allowed

Note : The case was decided partly in favour of the assessee.

the assessee the right to move this court for compelling the Commissioner to make reference on the ground that his case involves questions of law, and this Court on being satisfied that the Commissioners view that no questions of law are involved is not correct, can issue directions to him to state the case. It is sufficient for the purposes of the reference if the questions set forth in the petition to this Court arise out of the Commissioners order passed under section 31 or section 32 of the 1922 Act. Therefore an assessee is entitled to move the High Court for a direction to the Commissioner to refer questions of law raised by him in his petition to the High Court even though they may not have been raised before him in the course of the proceedings under section 66(2) provided that they are questions of law arising out of the Commissioners order passed in appeal.

Under section 22 and section 23(4) of the 1922 Act it is the duty of the assessee to supply the materials of his assessment. If he fails to supply or having supplied fails, to substantiate the same under section 23 (3) the ITO has still to assess the total income of the assessee to the best of his judgment as contemplated by section 23 (4) of the 1922 Act.

The assessee’s accounts being unclosed he was unable to supply the full material, much less to substantiate the same. Realizing this difficulty the assessee in his oral statement admitted that he had nothing to say if some fair percentage was adopted to find out his income. On the facts ascertained by the Assistant Commissioner in his enquiry assessee had no reason to think that the rate of 2 per cent was unreasonable and the Commissioner also had confirmed the same. The reasonableness or otherwise of the rate applied could not be a question of law which would be agitated. Had the assessee disputed in his statement the authority of the Income tax Department of adopt a flat rate, then question of law might have arisen for consideration as to whether in the absence of other reliable data as to income of an assessee from a certain source an ITO is justified in making an assessment based on a formula deduced by taking a certain percentage of the gross turn over, as representing a fair margin of profit. But on the admission made by the assessee in this behalf that question did not arise. Therefore, it followed that it was not open to him to argue merely the question of the unreasonableness of the extent of the percentage adopted.

As for as second item was concerned, it was an admitted fact that even though the liability for adat charges was incurred during the Samvat year 1978-79, the same had not been paid to the Adatya before the close of the year. The Commissioner was, therefore, right in disallowing this item as it was not expenditure incurred for earning the profits of the account year within the meaning of section 10(ix), or section 11(2) of the 1922 Act. No doubt it could be termed a liability incurred so long it was not satisfied. But it appeared the Income tax Act for obvious reasons did not take into account mere monitary obligation or liabilities incurred. The Commissioner was, therefore, right in refusing to allow the deduction. The sum paid on account of interest to others for the business would certainly be debitable against the gross income of the business under section 11(2). The Commissioner’s opinion showed that might have allowed those deductions had the assessee furnished the necessary details and shown that the payment made was before the end of the account year.

A part of this amount was paid after the assessment order was made, i.e., after the accounts were examined. Thus the Commissioner entertained doubts about the correctness of the debit and thought fit to disallow it.

It was held that an assessee is not entitled to deduct any expenditure not actually incurred by him before the close of the account year and that a deduction can be claimed only if the expenditure is actually incurred or the liability incurred is satisfied before the close of the year.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

A.V. Khare for the Applicant

D.N. Choudhary for the Respondent.

HEADNOTE: Section 145, read with section 256, of Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 13, read with section 66, of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Method of accounting - Estimation of profit - Assessee’s accounts were so complicated that its not for auditor could not prepare profit and loss statement therefrom - ITO assessed assessee at flat rate of 10 per cent on total turnover instead of 6¼ per cent as adopted for other similarly placed assessees - Whether charging of flat rate was only one mode of arriving at assessment in absence of clearly and properly kept accounts - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, no referable question of law arose from order of ITO - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm was assessed to income-tax, by applying a flat rate of 10 per cent on the total turnover. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner while maintaining the flat rate of 10 per cent reduce the amount on which the tax was to be assessed by the amount said to have been expended on the journeys to the East. In the application to the Commissioner made under section 66(2) of the 1922 Act, it was said that it was illegal for the department to raise arbitrarily in the petitioner’s case the flat rate of 6 1/4 per cent accepted and admitted by the Department itself as the basis for the purpose of assessment in the case of all wholesale dealers of silk. The Commissioner refused to refer this question as he did not consider it to be a question of law.

On application under section 66(3) of the 1922 Act :

HELD: The question sought to be referred by the assessee, was not a question of law. The charging of flat rate is only one mode of arriving at the assessment in the absence of clearly and properly kept accounts and in the instant case admittedly the accounts were so complicated that their auditor was unable to prepare a profit and loss account from them. There was no question of law which the High Court could possibly direct the Commissioner to refer.

The application was, accordingly, dismissed.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

Jagan Nath Aggarwal for the Assessee.

Government for the Crown.

HEADNOTE: Section 164 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 41(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Trust/trustees - Charge of tax where shares of beneficiaries unknown - Assessment years 1958-59 to 1961-62 - Deceased dedicated two of his properties as wakf properties under a deed of wakf - For assessment year 1958-59, ITO assessed income from wakf properties in status of 'AOP' and computed tax at maximum rate on ground that shares of beneficiaries under wakf were not determinate - In subsequent years also computation of tax was made at maximum rate - Whether assessment order of 1958-59 did not operate as assessment res-judicata for subsequent years - Held, yes - Whether failure to indicate reason for applying maximum rate of tax would not amount to such an infirmity as would justify quashing assessment order by a writ - Held, yes - Whether, however, where assessment at maximum rate was challenged in appeal, onus would have been on taxing authority to justify such computation - Held, yes

FACT: The deceased dedicated two premises under a deed of wakf. The income from the wakf estate was assessed for the assessment year 1958-59, treating the assessee as association of persons. The tax was computed at the maximum rate under the proviso to section 41(1), on the theory that the shares of the beneficiaries under the wakf were not determinate. For the assessment years 1959-60 to 1961-62, computation of tax on the income assessed was also made at the maximum rate without assigning any reason whatsoever.

On writ :

HELD: The order of assessment for the year 1958-59 did not operate as res judicata for the subsequent years could not amounts to such an infirmity in the assessment order as would justify in quashing the assessment order by a writ.

The maximum rate of tax may have been correctly applied on the assessment. There was nothing to show from the record that the application of the maximum rate must have been wrongly done. If the assessment had been challenged in appeal, the onus would have been on the taxing authority to justify the computation of tax at the maximum rate, in the facts and circumstances of the case. The failure to indicate the reasons for assessment at the maximum rate does not constituted such an infirmity in the order that it must be quashed.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 143 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Assessment - Estimate of income - Whether in view of fact that rice bran obtained in process of paddy milling could not be quantified by any uniform standard, and in absence of any evidence that assessee had made any sale of rice bran, any addition would be called for simply by postulating a slightly higher percentage of rice bran yield than that returned by assessee - Held, no

Section 143 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Assessment - Estimate of income - Assessee did not account for rice husk obtained in process of paddy milling on ground that it had no marketability and was consumed in dryer plant - Whether in view of various uses of such husk, it could be said that husk had no marketability and that assessee had not derived any pecuniary benefit from it - Held, no - Whether taking into consideration its marketability and fact that assessee had used it in its dryer plant as well, it would be reasonable to make addition of Rs. 15,000 instead of Rs. 98,000 determined by ITO - Held, yes

Section 28(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with section 11(8) of the Punjab General Sales Tax Act - Business loss/deductions - Allowability of -  Whether amount paid for non-payment of sales tax in time is tantamount to additional tax or compensatory interest and not penalty constituting infringement of law and is, thus, allowable as deduction - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a registered firm, engaged in the business of paddy milling. During the assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1982-83, the ITO noticed a difference in the percentage of rice bran obtained on the assessee’s own account and that obtained on account of the third parties. The shortage was quantified by him and an addition of Rs. 1,89,000 made. On the assessee challenging the addition in appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals), the ITO agreed to reduce the addition to Rs. 25,140 only on the basis of difference of 0.5 per cent between the yield of 3 per cent declared by the assessee and 3.5 per cent certified by one of the third parties. The Commissioner (Appeals), however, observed that in the milling process no uniform norm was set which could help to conclude that the yield could be only 3.5 per cent and not more or less, nor was there any evidence that the assessee had made any sale of rice bran out of the account books. Thus, holding the addition of Rs. 1,89,000 as having been made without any basis or material evidence, he deleted the same.

Secondary, the ITO made an addition of Rs. 98,000 on account of sale of rice husk at the rate of Rs. 7 per quintal. The assessee had shown the quantity of rice husk obtained from paddy milled on its own account, but had not shown the yield from paddy milled on account of the third parties. It had also not shown its sale, nor was its value accounted for in the closing stock on the ground that rice husk had no value. The ITO held that the commodity was marketable and its average price was Rs. 7 per quintal. Thus, he computed the value of the entire quantity of rice husk obtained by the assessee and made the above addition. On appeal, the assessee contended that the husk was burnt by it in its dryer plant and that the ITO had not explained the basis of his fixing the price at Rs. 7 per quintal. The revenue, per contra, contended that the assessee had not maintained any record regarding the production and consumption of husk and the sale price at Rs. 7 per quintal was the price prevalent at the relevant time. The Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition as having been made on surmises and without material evidence.

On appeal by the revenue :

HELD: The reasons given by the Commissioner (Appeals) ordering deletion of addition of Rs. 1,89,000, were tenable. Thus, it was to be held that the situation did not warrant confirmation of any addition. The finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) under challenge was, thus, confirmed.

In the present case, the Commissioner (Appeals) has rightly considered the fact that there has been sharp increase of 240 per cent in the turnover which has increased from Rs. 12.73 crores last year to Rs. 29.34 crores this year and to achieve such a tremendous increase, the assessee must have compromised with the margins which certainly justifies fall in the GP rate by 2.39 per cent to an extent. [Para 9] Further, past history is the best guide in the cases of estimation. The Commissioner (Appeals) also held that the past history would be most reliable guideline in this regard. However, it appears that the Commissioner (Appeals) has continued harping upon the increase in turnover and taking that factor alone has estimated GP rate at 9.50 per cent without further looking into the other contentions of the assessee and relevant factors though made available on record. He also did not provide any basis as to why application of GP rate at 9.50 per cent was justified. It is noticed that the assessee had provided specific reasons because of which the GP rate declared in this year has come down to 8.81 per cent as against 11.21 per cent declared in the last year, which aspect has been completely ignored by the Commissioner (Appeals). It is seen that out of the total turnover Rs. 29.34 crores the sale of Beedi was of Rs. 2,92,13,579 which constituted 10 per cent only of the total sale and rest of the sale was on account of Tendu Patta but there has been a substantial increase in the purchase rate of Tendu patta as shown by the assessee in the comparative chart placed in the assessee's paper book, according to which there has been increase of Rs. 964 per bag registering an increase of 83 per cent. On the other hand, however, the corresponding increase in selling price was only up to 45.25 per cent in as much as the average sale rate of Rs. 1,540 per bag in last year could increase up to Rs. 2,237 this year. This is evident from a chart placed in the assessee's paper book along with the copies of the purchase bills as also sale bills. Moreover, in Maharashtra State in the substantial purchases of Rs. 3,40,85,802 the assessee could earn a GP of 2.80 per cent only. There was no opening and closing stock in this account. This implies that the assessee could earn very low margin as compared to the preceding year. [Para 10]

In past various years, the Revenue itself has been applying a flat NP rate after rejecting the accounts and therefore, when the matter in various years reached up to the Tribunal, the Tribunal has also estimated the income based on the application of flat NP rate. Hence, there appears no justifiable reason nor the authorities below have ever justified, as to why in this year the Assessing Officer and Commissioner (Appeals) should have considered the GP rate only for making a comparison with past year/s. This year, the assessee declared NP rate of 3.98 per cent as against 3.37 per cent last year. From a perusal of the comparative NP chart starting from assessment year 2001-02 to the subjected assessment year 2008-09 and perusal of the various Tribunal orders placed in the assessee's paper book, it is noticed that the Tribunal has upheld even 0.50 per cent in assessment year 2004-05. Further, in assessment years 2005-06 to 2007-08 although assessments were completed under scrutiny under section 143(3) wherein the assessee declared NP rate ranging between 2 per cent to 3.40 per cent yet however, no trading addition appears to have been made. It is also noticed that in assessment year 2001-02 NP rate of 0.87 per cent and in assessment year 2003-04 NP rate at 1.60 per cent was declared and was upheld by the Tribunal. This year, the assessee declared NP rate at 3.98 per cent which is certainly better than NP rate at 3.37 per cent declared last year. In assessment year 2006-07 the assessee itself declared NP rate at 4.06 per cent, however, a better course would be, in the case of fair estimation, to consider an average of 2-3 years of the past as against comparing with the immediately preceding year alone. In assessment years 2005-06 to 2007-08 the turnover has been almost similar i.e., ranging between Rs. 12.50 lacs to Rs. 12.80 lacs and, therefore, it would be quite reasonable to consider average of the three years, which comes to 3.19 per cent. As against this the assessee has achieved a turnover of more than Rs. 29 crores with NP rate of 03.98 per cent this year.

HEADNOTE: Section  28(i)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961/ Section  26  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 - Business income – Chargeable as (Rate of tax) - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee-company was engaged in trading of IT products - Assessing Officer assessed commission income arising from impugned transactions under head 'Profits and Gains of Business or Profession' but computed tax liability applying a rate of 40% - Whether since commission income was assessed as business income, same had necessarily to be subjected to tax at rates applicable to assessee in respect of income chargeable under head 'Profits and Gains of Business or Profession', and not at any special or higher rate otherwise not applicable in law - Held, yes [Para 9.1] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee-company was engaged in trading of IT products and filed its return for A.Y. 2017-18 declaring NIL income. The case was selected for scrutiny and notices under sections 133(2) and 141(1) were issued.

■

The AO assessed commission income arising from the impugned transactions under the head 'Profits and Gains of Business or Profession' but computed tax liability applying a rate of 40%.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal, the assessee challenged the computation of tax on the business income at 40%.

HELD: ■

It is noted that the commission income assessed in the hands of the assessee has been treated by the authorities below as income chargeable under the head "Profits and Gains of Business or Profession". The AO, instead of making addition of the entire gross trade receipts arising out of the circular trading transactions, restricted the addition only to the extent of 1% of the turnover, treating the same as commission income earned by the assessee. [Para 9]

■

In such circumstances, once the income is assessed as business income, the same has necessarily to be subjected to tax at the rates applicable to the assessee in respect of income chargeable under the head "Profits and Gains of Business or Profession", and not at any special or higher rate otherwise not applicable in law. The AO is directed to apply the rate of tax applicable to the relevant head under which the commission income has been assessed. Accordingly, Ground No. 8 raised by the assessee is, therefore, partly allowed for statistical purposes. [Para 9.1]

brought under the statute. Thus the meaning of the turnover as provided under section 145A cannot be adopted while determining the rate of tax in pursuance to First Schedule of Finance (No. 2) Act, 2019 based on turnover. However, the Bench keeps this issue open and is not inclined to adjudicate at this juncture whether to include or exclude the amount of excise duty from the amount of turnover on the issue on hand. [Para 12.6] Similarly the ICAI does not mandate to include the amount of excise duty in the value of sales. [Para 12.7]

Likewise it is also important to note that the assessee is collecting the excise duty from the customers in the capacity of an agent only and does not give any rise to the income of the assessee. The Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. Lakshmi Machine Works [2007] 160 Taxman 404/290 ITR 667 had directed to exclude the excise duty from the amount of turnover. [Para 12.8]

Besides the above, the excise duty is leviable on manufacturing of the goods and the rate of the same varies based on different goods being manufactured. There can be a situation where a company manufactures goods subject to excise duty at the rate of 5 per cent, whereas another company manufacturing other goods and excise duty is applicable on the same at the rate of 25 per cent of the sales. Thus in a situation where both the companies having exact amount of sales but because of different rate of excise duty their turnover can be of different amount and consequently both the companies may fall under different tax bracket, i.e., 25 per cent or 30 per cent, as the case may be, which does not appear to be in consonance with the intent of article 14 of the Constitution of India. [Para 12.9]

In view of the aforesaid, the issue whether to include or exclude the excise from the amount of turnover for determining the rate of tax in pursuance to First Schedule of Finance (No. 2) Act, 2019 is a debatable issue which cannot be resolved in the intimation processed under section 143(1). [Para 12.10]

Therefore, the issue whether to include excise duty as a part of the turnover while applying the tax rate is a debatable issue and the same cannot be resolved while processing the return of income under section 143(1). [Para 12.11]

The Commissioner (Appeals) while adjudicating the issue has not made any reference to the turnover for the financial year 2016-17 which was required to be considered for working out the applicable tax rate. As such the Commissioner (Appeals) has adopted the turnover of the assessee for the year under consideration for working out the tax rate applicable to the assessee. [Para 12.12]

In view of the above, the adjustment made by the Assessing Officer while processing the return of income under section 143(1) in the given facts and circumstances is not sustainable being an issue of debatable nature. [Para 12.13]

subject matter of tax and the standard by which amount of tax is measured. The levy of tax is defined by its nature and the measure of tax may be assessed by its own standard. A standard may be adopted as the measure of levy and may indicate nature of the tax but would not necessarily determine it. Though the measure of tax is furnished by the method referred to under rule 58, it does not cease to be a tax on transfer of goods in a works contract. [Para 69] Where in construction contracts element of transfer of interest in land is involved, rule 58(1A) provides for mandatory method of computing the assessable value. The circular dated 21-2-2014 clarifies what has been provided in rule and as such is not ultra vires. Rule 58(1A) is mandatory and land cost has to be determined by the method and mode as is specified. It cannot be said that it is not a permissible method. Once it is permissible, it is open for the Legislature or its delegates to adopt one of those methods on principle of uniformity. It would be permissible for the State Legislature to prescribe a formula for determination of charges and to allow deductions of amount. Proviso to rule 58(1A) and rule 58(1B) were enacted to deal with such a situation. [Para 70]

The Government of Maharashtra has introduced the proviso giving an opening to the dealers to prove before the Department of Town Planning and Valuation that the actual cost of land is higher than that determined in accordance with the annual statement of rates (including guidelines) under the provisions of the Bombay Stamp (Determination of True Market Value of Property) Rules, 1995. Apprehension as such, that determination of land value pursuant to annual statement of rates may be different from actual cost, is taken care of and a remedy is made available. The proviso opens an avenue to the dealer to prove actual cost. It cannot be said that by such proviso tax assessed would not to be directed to the value of goods. Intention is to determine value on evidence produced about land cost. [Para 72]

Trade circulars dated 21-2-2014 and 17-4-2014 are clarificatory in nature and do not transgress the contours of rule 58. It cannot be said that the impugned circulars are bad or illegal or for that matter unconstitutional. Trade circular dated 17-4-2014 comprises responses to some frequently asked questions. The circulars clarify the mandate of statute and do not introduce a condition or restriction not found in the rule or statute. [Para 73]

While prescribing the modalities of valuation under rule 58 and particularly under rule 58(1),(1A) and (1B), the object all along appears to adopt a standard and measure for assessment of subject of tax and the object is neither lost sight of nor is obfuscated. The rule all along has in view and nexus with subject of tax. [Para 74]

Allegation with respect to the notification dated 29-1-2014 and rule 58(1A) and (1B) being bad for want of previous publication cannot be sustained. It cannot be said that the Government had no power, authority or jurisdiction to make the rules operative without previous publication. As such, it cannot be said that absence of previous publication would render the rule 58(1A) and (1B) defective, illegal, ultra vires or bad in law. [Para 75]

It is to be borne in mind that defining the subject of tax is a simple task and devising measure for tax is far more complex exercise and the Legislature has to be given much more flexibility in the latter field. Once having taken into account that it is competent of Legislature to make a choice and if it does so for the matters of uniformity and convenience, the rule and the circulars cannot be said to be ultra vires, unconstitutional or bad in law. Rule 58(1), (1A) and (1B) and rest of the rule is precisely intended to charge and collect levy of tax assessed pursuant to the same at the stages, as referred to. [Para 76]

Rule 58(1A) and (1B) cannot be said to travel beyond the parent Act or for that matter alters the character or nature of the tax. It cannot be said that the object underlying rule has no link and nexus with essential character of the tax being levied. [Para 83]

In the process, in some cases, if there is any over payment of tax, the provision makes allowance for its refund and would not tantamount to tax on land. [Para 84]

In view of the aforesaid, challenge to rule 58(1A) and (1B) and the trade circulars 7T of 2014 and 12T of 2014 is not sustainable. [Para 87]

HEADNOTE: Section 154, read with section 263, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Rectification of mistakes - Apparent from record - Assessment years 1972-73 and 1973-74 - Whether in absence of entire material on record for determining standard rent according to sections 6 and 7 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, ITO could not straightaway pass rectification order under section 154 automatically in each and every case on basis of Supreme Court judgments and, therefore, Commissioner would be justified in annulling said order under section 263 - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee’s income derived from house property, business, etc., for the assessment years 1972-73 and 1973-74 was assessed by the ITO under section 143(1). Subsequently in view of the Supreme Court judgments in cases Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Committee [1980] 122 ITR 700, Mrs. Sheila Kaushish v. CIT [1981] 131 ITR 435 and Amolak Ram Khosla v. CIT [1981] 131 ITR 589, the ITO rectified his earlier orders under section 154 by determining the annual letting value according to standard rent under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958. He calculated the annual letting value on the basis of 1/3rd of the cost of construction and land, as reflected in the balance sheets of the respective years. The Commissioner, invoking his powers under section 263, held the orders passed by the ITO to be erroneous and prejudicial to the interests of the revenue, inasmuch as there was no mistake apparent from record to be rectified and the issue involved was a debatable one.

On appeal :

HELD: The judgment of the Supreme Court, which is the law of the land, will entitle the ITO to rectify an order under section 154. After the judgment of the Supreme Court the whole controversy, if any, about the issue involved comes to an end and thereafter there is no debate left. Standard rent in different cases has to be worked out depending upon the facts of each case. For determining the standard rent under section 6 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, the material should be available on all the points mentioned therein. Nothing had been brought on record to show or discussed by the ITO in its order that material was available for determining the standard rent. The ITO had straightaway applied the percentage with reference to the balance sheet value as on 31-3-1972 and 31-3-1973, which was certainly not correct. Before resorting to that formally, the other aspects had to be considered. Even this determination was wrong as the ITO had not made any attempt to find out the cost of construction and the market value of the land on the date of commencement of construction. It was also not known whether the balance sheet values adopted by the ITO were after reducing depreciation claimed on building occupied for business purposes or the original value. Since no material was available on the record of the ITO for determining the standard rent under section 6 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, enquiry/investigation into facts was necessary. Hence, this could not be termed as a mistake apparent from record. The ITO, therefore, did not assume valid jurisdiction for passing orders under section 154. The orders having been passed without jurisdiction, the Commissioner was justified in annulling the same.

On second appeal :

HELD: The Assessing Officer had not pointed out any specific defect regarding correctness or completeness of accounts as envisaged under sub-section 145(3).
