sale, the tax collected will be held over. This is what sub-section (4) of section 206C says, and there is no illegality in saying so. It must be remembered that this is an anti-evasion measure. It is a specified provision designed to meet a specific situation. So long as the assessee trades in or does business in the goods purchased, tax can be levied and in the circumstances it will be levied in the year in which the goods are sold. As regards the violation of articles 14 and 19(1)(g ) of the Constitution of India, the Supreme Court in the case of V. Venugopala Rani Verma Rajah v. Union of India AIR 1969 SC 1094, has laid down that equal protection clause enshrined in article 14 is not an abstract proposition. Quite often laws are enacted with a view to solve specific problems, or to achieve definite objectives by specific remedies. In such a situation, absolute equality or uniformity of treatment is impossible of achievement. Tax Laws are aimed at dealing with complex problems of infinite variety necessitating adjustment of several disparate elements. The Courts accordingly admit, subject to adherence to the fundamental principles of the doctrine of equality, a larger play to legislative discretion in the matter of classification. The power to classify may be exercised so as to adjust the system of taxation in all proper and reasonable ways; the Legislature may select persons, properties, transactions and objects, and apply different methods and even rates for tax, if the Legislature does so reasonably. Protection of the equality clause does not predicate a mathematically precise or logically complete or symmetrical classification; it is not a condition of the guarantee of equal protection that all transactions, properties, objects or persons of the same genus must be affected by it or none at all. If the classification is rational, the Legislature is free to choose objects of taxation, impose different rates, exempt classes of property from taxation, subject different classes of property to tax in different ways and adopt different modes of assessment. A taxing statute may contravene article 14 of the Constitution if it seeks to impose on the same class of property, persons, transactions or occupations similarly situate, incidence of taxation, which leads to obvious inequality. A taxing statute is not, therefore, exposed to attack on the ground of discrimination merely because different rates of taxation are prescribed for different categories of persons, transactions, occupations or objects. It is for the Legislature to determine the objects on which tax shall be levied, and the rates thereof. The Courts will not strike down an Act as denying the equal protection of laws merely because other objects could have been, but are not, taxed by the Legislature. Thus, section 44AAC and section 206C does not suffer from any constitutional infirmity.

HEADNOTE: Section 254, read with section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 33(4), read with section 13 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Appellate Tribunal - Order of - Assessment years 1943-44 to 1945-46 - Assessee-firm carried on business of aerodrome work, katcha building constructions etc. - On firm's failure to produce books of account for relevant assessment years, ITO took sum total of receipts of assessee for three accounting years and, thereupon adopted profit rate of 40 per cent in exercise of his power under section 13, read with section 23(4) of 1922 Act - Tribunal, however, opined that ITO should have applied rate of profit to annual receipts instead of total receipts and that by amalgamating receipts under one assessment ITO raised tax liability of assessee which was not fair - Besides, Tribunal also reduced profit rate from 40 per cent to 30 per cent - Whether Tribunal was right in asking ITO to assess assessee on receipt basis with regard to contracts carried out and completed during year of accounting, there being every presumption that incomes were paid as soon as they became due - Held, yes - Whether, however, as regards reduction of flat rate of profit, Tribunal did commit a mistake of law in arriving at said finding for which there was no relevant evidence to support - Held, yes

FACT: Two persons 'S' and B constituted an unregistered firm sharing the profits and losses in the proportion of 9-as and 7-as respectively. The business, of which the profits and gains were the subject of assessment, consisted of aerodrome work under the Central Public Works Department, certain katcha building constructions under the Military Engineering Service and small supply of potatoes to Garrison Engineer. During the accounting year 1942-43, the assessee received a sum of Rs. 2,92,256. During the next year, that is 1-4-1943 to 31-3-1944, they received a sum of Rs. 86,434 and during the following accounting year of 1-4-1944 to 31-3-1945, they received a sum of Rs. 25,703. Besides it appeared, there were certain estimated outstanding bills to the credit of the assessee which had been excluded from assessment. On firm's failure to produce, books of account, the ITO took the sum total of the above sums received in course of three years, that is Rs. 4,54,948, as the basis of his assessment. He deducted the income at Rs. 1,18,975, on the ratio of 40 per cent, a flat rate on the gross receipts. Deducting the excess profits tax of Rs. 1,13,317 the assessable income was set at Rs. 65,659 which was reduced by the AAC by a sum of Rs. 28,270 by way of rectification of an error in calculation of Rs. 24,270 and deducting the profits of Rs. 4,000 representing 40 per cent of the estimated outstanding bills. The AAC, on appeal, came to the conclusion that since it was a question of determination of that year's income, in the absence of account books and since this was the first assessment in the case, the proviso to section 13 came into operation and no question of cash basis could arise.

The Tribunal, however, thought that in the circumstances of the case, the ITO should have applied the rate of profit to the annual receipts instead of to the total receipts and that by amalgamating the receipts under one assessment the ITO raised the tax liability of the assessee which was not fair. The Tribunal, therefore, set aside the basis of the said assessment and remanded the case back to the ITO to assess the income on the basis of the receipts during each year.

On the question of the flat rate, the Tribunal reduced the estimate of 40 per cent to 30 per cent.

According to the section, every order of assessment passed by an AAC either under section 28 or section 31 of 1922 Act, is appealable to the Tribunal. The latter can substitute its own order of assessment for the one passed by the appellate income-tax authority. This very widely expressed power, however, shall not be immune from such limitation to which ordinarily an appellate authority or tribunal is subject in the disposal of its duty.

On appeal the question for consideration was whether sub-section (10) which was introduced through Finance Act, 1956with retrospective effect from 1-4-1956 could apply to an assessment which had been made before sub-section (10) came into force.

HELD: Per Court (Majority Judgment) The Income-tax Act imposes a charge of tax for a year at a time and that year is the year of assessment. The charge is in respect of a previous year which is commonly known as the year of account. The rate at which the tax is to be charged is enacted by an annual Finance Act for each assessment year. The assessment year is the financial year. From the nature of things an amendment of the Income-tax Act, made in the middle of the assessment year, if made to operate from the beginning of the assessment year, operates on incomes which had been earned before. Since an amendment cannot be allowed to operate from the mid - term, each such amendment is made to comprise a whole assessment year whether it be the assessment year then running or an earlier or a latter assessment year. Amendments are thus given retrospective operation from the first day of April in the same or a preceding, or prospective operation for a future assessment year. Ordinarily, the law, as it stands on the 1st of April in any assessment year, applies to assessments in that year but the law may expressly or by necessarily implication give itself a greater retrospective operation.

The date on which the amendment comes into force is the date of the commencement of the amendment. It is read as amended from that date. Under ordinarily circumstances, an Act does not have retrospective operation on substantial right which have became fixed before the date of the commencement of the Act. But this rule is not unalterable. The legislature may affect substantial rights by enacting laws which are expressly retrospective or by using language which has that necessary result. And this language may give an enactment more retrospectively than what the commencement clause gives to any of its provisions. When this happens the provisions thus made retrospective, expressly or by necessary intendment, operate from a date earlier than the date of commencement and affect rights which, but for such operation, would have continued undistributed.

If the Income-tax Act prescribes a period during which the tax due in any particular assessment year may be assessed, then on the expiry of that period the department cannot make an assessment . Where no period is prescribed the assessment can be completed at any time but once completed it is final. Once a final assessment has been made, it can only be reopened to rectify a mistake apparent from the record (section 35) or to reassess where there has been an escapement of assessment of income for one reason or another (section 34). Both these sections, which enable reopening of back assessments, provide their own periods of time for action but all these periods of time, whether for the first assessment or for rectification, or for re-assessment, merely create a bar when that time passed against the machinery set up by the Act for the assessment and levy of the tax. They do not create an exemption in favour of the assessee or grant an absolution on the expiry of the period. The liability is not enforceable but the tax may again become exigible if the bar is removed and the taxpayer is brought within the jurisdiction of the said machinery by reason of a new power. This is, of course, subject to the condition that the law must say that such is the jurisdiction, either expressly or by clear implication. If the language of the law has that clear meaning, it must be given that effect and where the language expressly so declares or clearly implies it, the retrospective operation is not controlled by the commencement clause.

The concerned amendment was made by the Finance Act, 1956. By section 2, it dealt with the year beginning on 1-4-1956, and fixed the rates of tax for the assessment year commencing on that date. It also amended the Income-tax Act by sections 3 to 35. Section 28 then prescribed the dates of commencement of these sections. It said that the amendments made in the Income-tax Act by section 4 and section 15(b) shall be deemed to have come into force on 1-4-1955, and the amendments made by sections 3 to 27 inclusive shall come into force on 1-4-1956.

Sub-section (10) was introduced into section 35 of the Income-tax Act by section 19 of this Act. If there was nothing more in the language of the sub-section to give it operation from an earlier date it would have operated only from 1-4-1956, but the language of the sub-section gives it additional retrospectivity and says so in such clear and unambiguous language as to leave no doubt.

HEADNOTE: Section 144 of the income-tax act, 1961-Best judgment assessment-Whether ex parte ASSESSMENT vitiated when ITO's guess work about income was found to be arbitrary and without giving basis for computation-Held, yes

FACT: The assessee filed his income-tax return on estimate basis by adopting flat rate of 10 per cent on gross contract receipts, while the ITO adopted flat rate of 15 per cent thereon. The assessee's revision petition before the Commissioner was unsuccessful.

On writ petition:

HELD: It is now well settled that, while making a best judgment assessment, the guess work must not be arbitrary. Neither the ITO nor the Commissioner has referred to any material for applying flat rate of 15 per cent while estimating net profits. The basis for computation is also not disclosed in the assessment order. The assessment order, thus, cannot but be held to be arbitrary. The impugned orders were, accordingly, set aside and the ITO was held to be at liberty to make fresh assessment in accordance with the law.

Section 143 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Assessment - Additions to income - Assessment year 1996-97 - Assessee claimed to have received interest at rate of 18 per cent from its various customers against pawned jewellery - Assessing Officer, however, on basis of seized material recovered during search which was conducted at assessee’s premises held that interest was received by assessee at 24 per cent and, accordingly, charged interest at said rate - Whether in view of decision of Tribunal in assessee’s own case addition made to income of assessee by charging interest at higher rate of 24 per cent was to be deleted - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee claimed to have received interest at the rate of 18 per cent from its various customers against the pawned jewellery. The Assessing Officer, however, on the basis of seized material recovered during search, which was conducted at premises of assessee, and following the order for the assessment year 1994-95 held that interest was received by the assessee at 24 per cent. The Assessing Officer, accordingly, enhanced the income by charging the interest at 24 per cent as against 18 per cent interest shown by the assessee. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed to apply interest of 21 per cent against the 24 per cent interest charged by the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

HELD: In view of the decision of the Tribunal in assessee’s own case, the order of the lower authorities was set aside and it was directed that interest at the rate of 18 per cent as disclosed by the assessee was to be charged.

Whether since AO after establishing business connection, had applied beneficial provision of article 7, both Assessing Officer as well as Commissioner were on same page and insofar as application of law was concerned, Assessing Officer had taken a very plausible view supported by relevant provisions of Act and, therefore, impugned assessment order could not be said to be erroneous and prejudicial to interest of revenue - Held, yes [Paras 16 and 18] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■ The assessee was a company incorporated in UAE and was a tax resident of UAE. The assessee was engaged in the business of operation of ships in international traffic and its operations were covered by article 8 of DTAA between India and UAE. During the year under consideration, the assessee received certain amount in the form of freight income, terminal handling charges, inland haulage charges and detention charges in India but the same was not offered to tax on the ground that the same was exempt under article 8 of the India – UAE DTAA.

■

The Assessing Officer found that the assessee was not able to produce any chartered agreements/ownership documents or pooling agreements for part of the amount and since the assessee was not able to submit supporting documents, the exemption under article 8 was denied to the assessee to that extent.Proceeding further, the activity of inland transportation was not considered as international transport and, accordingly, inland haulage charges were taxed under section 44B.

■

The Commissioner invoked section 263 on the ground that the Assessing Officer had taken income as per provisions of rule 10 of the Rules on the basis of net profit ratio of 3.53 per cent of gross receipts instead of computing income at 7.5 per cent as per section 44B which is a substantial provision.

■

On appeal:

HELD: ■

The entire case of the revenue revolves around wrong application of the tax rate which means that, there is no error insofar as the facts are concerned. Now, the only issue which needs consideration is whether the impugned assessment order is erroneous in law i.e., the moot point for consideration is whether the impugned assessment order is contrary to the provisions of law. [Para 11]

■

After establishing business connection, which has not been disputed by the assessee, the Assessing Officer applied the beneficial provision basis of Article 7. Since the Assessing Officer has taken a very plausible view supported by the relevant provisions of the Act and Rules, it can not be accepted that the impugned assessment order is erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of the revenue. [Para 16]

■

In light of the above, insofar as the facts are concerned, both the Assessing Officer as well as the Commissioner are on the same page and insofar as the application of law is concerned, the Assessing Officer has taken a very plausible view. Therefore, it is opined that the assessment order is neither erroneous nor prejudicial to the interest of the revenue. [Para 18]

■

It is a settled position of law that powers under section 263 can be exercised by the Commissioner on satisfaction of twin conditions, i.e., the assessment order should be erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of the Revenue. By 'erroneous' is meant contrary to law. Thus, this power cannot be exercised unless the Commissioner is able to establish that the order of the Assessing Officer is erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of the revenue. Thus, where there are two possible views and the Assessing Officer has taken one of the possible views, no action to exercise powers of revision can arise, nor can revisional power be exercised for directing a fuller enquiry to find out if the view taken is erroneous. This power of revision can be exercised only where no enquiry, as required under the law, is done. It is not open to enquire in case of inadequate inquiry. [Para 19]

■

Considering the facts of the case in totality, there is no error or infirmity in the assessment order which could make it erroneous to the interest of the revenue. Therefore, the order of the Commissioner is set aside and that of the Assessing Officer is restored. [Para 20]

The Commissioner (Appeals) had recorded a finding of fact that the assessee-company had made valuation of closing stock on the higher side. That being so, by making valuation of closing stock on higher side, the profits of the assessee-company stood automatically disclosed on a higher side than what it could be supposed to have earned. From this factor alone, estimation of profit at a higher rate was not at all justified. As regards estimation of total receipts and applicability of profit rate, there were no serious errors in accounts of the assessee-company found as a result of scrutiny of assessment made by the Assessing Officer. The job charges taken by the assessee-company had not been found under-stated nor was any enquiry conducted by the Assessing Officer from any of the parties to establish its case. Higher consumption of electricity in the year under appeal was a mere reference without looking into the actual consumption and the slabs processed by the assessee-company which warranted more consumption of electricity in the year under appeal in view of higher job work declared by the assessee-company. In view of these facts and circumstances, the total receipts taken at Rs. 10 lakhs appeared to be at a higher side. The assessee-company, however, had not challenged the application of the provisions of section 145. In the assessment year 1992-93 even after the decision by the Commissioner (Appeals) the Assessing Officer himself had accepted a profit rate of 20 per cent. Keeping in view the totality of the facts and circumstances and the submissions of the assessee-company as well as past history of the assessee-company’s case, it was fair and reasonable to estimate the total receipts at Rs. 9.25 lakhs and apply a profit rate of 20 per cent on estimate basis.

EDITOR’S NOTE

The Tribunal observed that the Commissioner (Appeals) exceeded his jurisdiction by deviating from the principal issue by entering into arena of scope of duties and liabilities of auditors which, in fact, would not have influenced trading results of assessee-company. Therefore, remarks and observations of the Commissioner (Appeals) against auditors which were nugatory and not relevant to issue at hand besides being perverse, were expunged by the Tribunal.

Sunil Goyal, O.P. Agarwal and Manish Agarwal for the Appellant. G.C. Bansal for the Respondent.

For purposes of determination of the annual letting value under clause (a) of section 23(1), the first question that is expected to be pondered by the Assessing Officers is as to whether the property is subject to the statutory controls under the relevant Rent Control Act. In case the relevant provisions of the Rent Control Act are applicable, the Assessing Officer is bound to determine the standard rent of the premises in accordance with provisions of that Act. Where the standard rent has been determined by the rent control authority, the Assessing Officer shall have no difficulty in ascertaining the standard rent as determined by such authority. However, where the standard rent has not been determined by the rent control authority, the Assessing Officer is duty bound to do the exercise himself and determine the standard rent as per the provisions of the relevant Rent Control Act. The decision in Diwan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Committee [1980] 122 ITR 700 (SC), is an authority for the proposition that the rateable value of the building is limited by the measure of the standard rent arrived at by the assessing authority by applying the principles laid down in the Rent Act and cannot exceed the figure of the standard rent so arrived at by the assessing authority. However, section 23 has been amended with effect from 1-4-1985, which provides for assessment of the annual letting value on the basis of expected rental value or the actual rent received or receivable whichever is higher. Therefore, after determination of the standard rent as per the provisions of the relevant Rent Control Act the Assessing Officer has got to find out as to what is the actual rent received or receivable by the owner. If the rent received is more than the standard rent, then the actual rent received has got to be assessed as the annual letting value of the house property. If the rent received is lower, then the standard rent shall be deemed to be the annual value of the house property.

facts.text:
The assessee was a military contractor. During the relevant accounting period, the assessee took three military engineering service contracts. The ITO found that the expenditure of the assessee was not supported by vouchers and he detected some other mistakes also in the accounts. After applying the provisions of section 145(1), the ITO assessed the profit from these contracts by applying a flat rate of 10 per cent on the total receipts. The AAC allowed the appeal of the assessee and held that no rate of profit could be applied on the value of the stores supplied by the Government and this order was upheld by the Tribunal.

On reference, the Division Bench noticed the divergent views taken by the various High Courts and particularly because of the challenge laid to the correctness of the judgment in Brij Bhushan Lal v. CIT [1971] 81 ITR 497 (Punj.) and, thus, referred the matter for decision of the Full Bench.

The assessee had income from sale of goods and also from money lending business. For the assessment year 1934-35, the assessee produced his books which showed only that he had sold a certain quantity of goods but they did not show as to what profits were obtained by the assessee. Under these circumstances the ITO assessed the profits at a flat rate of 12½ per cent on sale proceeds making allowances for legitimate expenses. The Assistant Commissioner and the commissioner were of the opinion that no further allowance in the shape of expenses could be allowed under the circumstances of the case, because the flat rate adopted by the ITO took into consideration all admissible expenses.

On reference:

The assessee was running a shop and was engaged in the activity of selling sweets, namkeen, samosa, milk and curd etc. He filed his return of income for the relevant assessment year and declared his taxable income at Rs.50,720 on the basis of the total turnover of Rs.11.56 lakhs.

During the course of assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer while completing the assessment recomputed the income of the assessee and declared his total income at Rs.13.66 lakhs. The assessee raised objections against the assessment order passed by the Assessing Officer and he also raised objections regarding the tax rate of samosa. The assessee contended that samosa would come under the category of Sweets and Namkeen, therefore it had to be taxed at the rate of 5 per cent and he also submitted that in fact Samosa in respect of the adjoining shop, had been taxed at 4 per cent under the entry 'Sweets and Namkeen'. But the Assessing Officer wrongly taxed the same at the rate of 8 per cent.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the contentions of the assessee and upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On further appeal, the Tribunal also upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On appeal to the High Court:

The assessee carried on business as a money-lender, and he also dealt in gold and silver. He kept no books of account, and therefore, the ITO was not able to ascertain with accuracy what the profits were from the sales of gold and silver, but in the years of assessment 1932-33 (Savrat year 1987) the ITO added to the assessee’s income 3 per cent on the sale of gold and 5 per cent on the sale of silver, and on that basis made the assessment under section 23(3). In the next year of assessment a different ITO dealing with the matter came to the conclusion that, as the price of gold had risen very rapidly during the last two months of the previous year of assessment, the ITO for that year had underestimated the profits derived from the sale of gold; he considered that the flat rate on sale of gold should have been 15 per cent, instead of 3 per cent, and on that basis he came to the conclusion that income had escaped assessment for the year 1932-33, and he therefore, re-assessed the income under section 34. The Assistant Commissioner, agreed generally with the view taken by the ITO but assessed income on the sale of gold at 4 per cent and on the sale of silver at 10 per cent and made an assessment on that basis.

On reference:

The assessee’s income derived from house property, business, etc., for the assessment years 1972-73 and 1973-74 was assessed by the ITO under section 143(1). Subsequently in view of the Supreme Court judgments in cases Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Committee [1980] 122 ITR 700, Mrs. Sheila Kaushish v. CIT [1981] 131 ITR 435 and Amolak Ram Khosla v. CIT [1981] 131 ITR 589, the ITO rectified his earlier orders under section 154 by determining the annual letting value according to standard rent under the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958. He calculated the annual letting value on the basis of 1/3rd of the cost of construction and land, as reflected in the balance sheets of the respective years. The Commissioner, invoking his powers under section 263, held the orders passed by the ITO to be erroneous and prejudicial to the interests of the revenue, inasmuch as there was no mistake apparent from record to be rectified and the issue involved was a debatable one.

On appeal :

The deceased dedicated two premises under a deed of wakf. The income from the wakf estate was assessed for the assessment year 1958-59, treating the assessee as association of persons. The tax was computed at the maximum rate under the proviso to section 41(1), on the theory that the shares of the beneficiaries under the wakf were not determinate. For the assessment years 1959-60 to 1961-62, computation of tax on the income assessed was also made at the maximum rate without assigning any reason whatsoever.

On writ :

The assessee filed his income-tax return on estimate basis by adopting flat rate of 10 per cent on gross contract receipts, while the ITO adopted flat rate of 15 per cent thereon. The assessee's revision petition before the Commissioner was unsuccessful.

On writ petition:

For the year 1998-99 the assessee filed returns disclosing rate of tax on cattle feeds @ 3%, whereas the rate of tax on the item was fixed at 4% w.e.f. 1.4.1998 as per the Finance Act 1998. The assessing authority did not object to the same until the final assessment for the year was completed as per order dated 3.4.2001. In the assessment order, the assessing authority levied an interest of Rs.9926. The first appellate authority allowed the appeal filed by the assessee. In appeal filed by the State, the Appellate Tribunal set aside the order of the first appellate authority and the order of the assessing authority levying penal interest was restored. On revision, the High Court:

In the returns filed for the period April, 2005 to March, 2006, the assessee had disclosed inter-State sale and paid tax at the rate of 4 per cent. It stated that it would furnish 'C' form in respect of said sale.

In the course of assessment proceedings, the assessee could not produce 'C' form. Thereupon the Assessing Authority levied tax at higher rate on sale in question.

He also levied interest under section 9(2B) from the date of furnishing of the returns.

The assessee had not disputed the levy of tax at the higher rate and paid the same.

The Tribunal held that interest could only be charged after issuance of the assessment order and not from the date of furnishing of the monthly returns.

On revision:

The assessee was engaged in the kirana business both on wholesale and retail basis. During the assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer, after pointing out that quantitative details and stock register were not maintained, invoked the provisions of section 145 and applied gross profit rate of 10 per cent on estimated sales and thereby, made an addition. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) applied gross profit rate at 9 per cent, after considering the fact that gross profit rate shown at 8.3 per cent was low in that line of business and partly deleted the addition.

On second appeal :

The assessee was running a rice sheller. It had filed the income-tax return for the relevant assessment year. The Assessing Officer completed the assessment, by making addition of Rs. 57,74,857 on account of processing of unaccounted rice bran and Rs. 3,52,260 on account of under-valuation of closing stock of rice bran. On second appeal, the Tribunal had adopted the flat rate of 10 per cent for working out the unaccounted profits and, thus, the assessment was made on estimate basis. In the meanwhile, the penalty proceedings were initiated by the Assessing Officer against the assessee under section 271(1)(c) for furnishing inaccurate particulars of income. On further appeal, the Tribunal set aside the order of penalty.

On revenue's appeal :

While completing the assessment for the assessment years 1936-37 to 1938-39, the Department under section 13, applied the rate of 20 per cent in respect of profits from the Military department contracts and 15 per cent in respect of the other two, because it was not possible from the accounts to work out what the actual net profits were. The department further held that the applicant was to be assessed as an individual and not as a Hindu joint family. The Commissioner also held that the expenditure upon the leases should be treated as capital expenditure and refused to state a case under section 66(2).

On an application under section 66(3):

A search was conducted at the premises of ‘S’ and allied concerns of the assessee. The main source of the assessee’s income was from pawning of jewellery. The assessee had shown interest income from pawning at the rate of 18 per cent per annum. The Assessing Officer enhanced the rate of interest to 24 per cent per annum on the basis of seized material, and accordingly made the addition. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) applied the rate of 21 per cent per annum.

On cross appeals :

The assessee was a wholesale dealer in solid spices for the relevant assessment year – Gross profit rate disclosed was 6-7 per cent. The ITO found that although the books of account were maintained, no day-to-day stock analysis was found. He also cited a comparable case of a dealer who, had dealt in powder spices as well as in solid spices and had shown 22.2 per cent gross profit for solid spices. The ITO, basing his judgment on the said case, rejected the book version of the profit of the assessee and applied a flat rate of 10 per cent and added a sum of Rs. 31,056.

On appeal, the Deputy Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal held that the ITO, on the basis of the case cited, had come to the conclusion that the profit shown by the assessee was low. Therefore, the Tribunal confirmed the addition.

On reference:

The assessee-company derived its income from the production and sale of rice bran extraction and the manufacture of laundry soap. By running two Solvent Extraction Units for the extraction of rice bran oil, the rice bran oil was being sold to various parties outside the territory of Punjab. While despatching the same to those parties, the assessee charged central sales tax from the buyers at the rate of 1 per cent only treating it as an edible oil, though for a non-edible oil, it should be 4 per cent. This realisation of 1 per cent was paid by the assessee to the sales tax authorities. Subsequently, the sales tax authorities held that rice bran oil was liable to be taxed at the rate of 4 per cent. The assessee’s appeal against this order was pending in the High Court. For the assessment year 1982-83, the assessee, however, claimed certain amount representing estimated sales tax liability to the extent of difference between 4 per cent and 1 per cent on account of rice bran oil sold to certain parties after hydrogenation on which sales tax at the rate of 1 per cent had been charged and paid.

The IAC (Assessment) rejected the assessee’s claim on the ground that no claim had been raised by the sales tax authorities at the rate of 4 per cent. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) while confirming the disallowance, observed that the assessee was free to claim the deduction as and when the liability got finalised.

On second appeal:

For the assessment of the year 1926-27, the assessee made a return of income in which he stated that he was a partner in two firms and that he had no other income. In response to a notice under section 23(2) of the 1922 Act the assessee admitted to the ITO that he had income from investments in Chetti firms in Burma and from moneys lent out and that he had no accounts or other evidence to prove the amount of such income. The ITO therefore acting to the best of his judgment, estimated the assessee’s income from money-lending. Subsequently the ITO found that the appropriate rate of tax was 18 pies (and not 1 anna in the rupee as was assumed in the original assessment). He, accordingly, issued a notice under section 34 of the 1922 Act. After considering assessee’s reply, ITO reassessed the income and levied additional tax. The appeal to the Assistant Commissioner was also dismissed.

On reference , the assessee submitted that when there are various heads under which a person returns his income, if in respect of one of those heads, owing to an omission or under-estimation he has been taxed at a certain rate which is subsequently found to be incorrect and notice is given to him under section 34 of the 1922 Act, the Income-tax Officer is not to confine himself to that portion which has escaped assessment but he is to begin again as if the notice sent was a first notice sent to the assessee to return his income.

The assessee submitted the return for the relevant period and paid tax on the sale of the goods at the rate of 4 per cent.

The Assessing Authority accepted the return and made assessment based thereon.

Subsequently the Audit Officer raised an objection to the effect that the rate of tax on the goods sold by the assessee was 12.5 per cent.

Thereupon the Assessing Authority reassessed the assessee and imposed tax on the sale of goods in question at the rate of 12.5 per cent. He also imposed penalty upon the assessee under section 21(2).

On writ :

The assessee made purchases of Rs. 95.26 lakhs from Mandi vendors.

The Assessing Officer was made an addition of Rs. 95.26 lakhs by considering purchases bogus.

The Commissioner (Appeals) partly sustained the addition by directing that the GP rate of 15 per cent be applied as against 9.27 per cent declared by the assessee.

On appeal before the Tribunal:

There was no specific entry in the First Schedule to cover tarpaulin as a classified item taxable at the rate provided therein during Assessment years 1982-83, 1983-84 & 1985-86. During the relevant point of time, relevant item in the Third Schedule (goods exempted from tax under section 9) was as follows: "7. Cotton fabrics, woollen fabrics and rayon or artificial silk fabrics as defined in items Nos. 19, 21 and 22 respectively of the First Schedule to the Central Excise and Salt Act 1944". In the absence of any specific entry, tarpaulin was covered by entry 7 of the Third Schedule. (Paras 5 & 6)

Assessment - Rate of tax - Clarification by government - Statutory provision granting unguided power to executive to decide upon rate of tax - Arbitrary -ultravires - Kerala General Sales Tax Act, 1963 section 59A; constitution of India, article 14.

The assessee was a registered firm carrying on construction business. It declared net profit of 5 per cent on gross receipts. The Assessing Officer applied the rate of 7 per cent subject to allowance of depreciation and interest on the basis of past history of assessee as well as the defective position of accounts. The Commissioner (Appeals) viewed that the normal rate of profit in construction business was 10 per cent and he, accordingly, applied 10 per cent rate relying on a case, purported to be a comparable case.

On second appeal :

The assessee-firm was a dealer in medicines. During the search conducted at business premises of assessee, certain purchase vouchers were found which were not recorded in the regular books of account. Similarly, certain papers were found which showed that some sales had also not been recorded. The ITO took recourse to proviso to section 145 and by applying the GP rate of 10 per cent, estimated the assessee’s income. Since the assessed income was more than double the income disclosed, the ITO imposed the penalty under section 271(1)(c).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted a part of penalty. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order of the Commissioner (Appeals).

On reference :

The assessee was a contractor undertaking project of Indian Railways on turnkey basis. A search action under section 132 was carried out at the assessee's premises. As the assessee, at the relevant point of time, was not able to collect information about such contracts or produce relevant personnel, it proposed for fixing net profit rate at 11 per cent. The Assessing Officer, accordingly, applied net profit rate at the rate of 11 per cent on the total contract receipts on estimate basis which however, was reduced to 8 per cent by the Tribunal. A penalty under section 271(1)(c) was also levied upon the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the penalty on the ground that the estimation of income by applying flat net profit ratio did not tantamount to concealment or filing inaccurate particulars of income.

On revenue's appeal:

Assessment for the assessment year 1992-93 had been made under section 143(1)(a) at returned income. The Commissioner found that the assessment was made without invoking section 44AC. He, therefore, held that the assessment order was erroneous, insofar as it was prejudicial to the interests of the revenue, and issued show-cause notice under section 263. The Commissioner rejected the assessee’s contention that there was no error in the assessment order in view of the decision of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in A. Sanyasi Rao v. Government of Andhra Pradesh [1989] 178 ITR 31/ 43 Taxman 271 and the decision of the Supreme Court in A. Sanyasi Rao’s case (supra), and directed the Assessing Officer to modify the assessment order and re-compute the taxable income of the assessee in the light of section 44AC read with sections 28 to 43C.

On appeal :

The assessee filed an application under section 59(4) seeking clarification of the rate of tax applicable on the following commodities: Vegit-Aloo Hara Bara Kebab, Vegit-Aloo Veg Cutlet, Vegit-Aloo Yummy Cheese Balls, Vegit-Aloo Mazedar Bonda and Vegit-Aloo Jatpat Tikki.

The Commissioner clarified that the commodities in question were unscheduled goods liable to tax at 12.5 per cent up to 31-3-2010 and at 13.5 per cent from 1-4-2010.

The Single Judge of the High Court held that the commodities in question were processed vegetables falling under Entry No. 3 of the Third Schedule and as such exigible to levy of tax at the rate of 4 per cent.

On writ appeal:

The petitioner manufactures wheat products like atta, rava andmaida from wheat which is purchased from Food Corporation of India or from wheat growing States like Punjab, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, etc. For the assessment year 1993-94, the assessing officer, proposed to levy the basic rate of tax at 2 per cent on the wheat products of atta, ra va and maida manufactured during the year out of the imported wheat purchased from outside the State plus usual incidental taxes like additional tax/turnover tax and surcharge.

The appellant assessee was carrying on business of timber merchant. In response to a notice under section 22(2) the assessee filed a return of income. The Officer refused to accept this return, and to test its accuracy called, under section 23(2), for evidence in its support. In response, the appellant’s business books were produced. From them it appeared that his sales of timber therein recorded for the year in question had been omitted. These further sales, although so effected, were not brought into charge until the month of April, 1927, after the expiration, that was to say, of the previous year. With these sales included in that year, as the ITO held they ought to have been, the appellant’s total sales for the year amounted to Rs. 5,27,958, and on the basis of that figure of sales the officer assessed the appellant to income-tax in respect of his business profit.

The ITO in order to arrive at the appellant’s profits from his business, applied a flat rate of 32.5 per cent to the above sum, stating, in his order of assessment, that no profit and loss account had been prepared by the appellant and that the rate of profit could not be deduced from his books. This rate was objected to by the appellant. His objection was not to a flat rate as such, but to this particular flat rate as being excessive and in the circumstances unwarranted. On appeal the Assistant Commissioner upheld the findings of the ITO. On reference the High Court held that the findings of the ITO and of the Assistant Commissioner as to the appellant’s system of accounting were findings of fact, based upon evidence. As to the assessment at flat rate of profit of 32.5 per cent they pointed out that no objection had been taken by the appellant to the same assessment for the two preceding years, 1924-25 and 1925-26 and it had not been shown that the ITO was not well warranted in maintaining the same percentage in respect of the year of assessment. The question was one of fact from him to decide.

On appeal to the Privy Council:

The assessee-firm was carrying on a business in potatoes and onions as a wholesale dealer. While framing assessment for the relevant assessment years the ITO held that the account books maintained by the assessee were unreliable. The ITO, therefore, made additions to the income disclosed by the assessee by applying a G.P. rate of 7.5 percent on estimated sales. On appeal, the AAC partly allowed the appeal by reducing the G.P. rate to 6 percent. On further appeal, the Tribunal directed the ITO to apply a G.P. rate of 6 percent on the declared sales of the assessee. On instant reference, the assessee contended that the Tribunal failed to take into consideration the provisions of the Madhya Pradesh Essential Articles (Exhibition of Prices and Price Control) Order, 1973. It was urged that in view of the provisions of the control order, the assessee could not have obtained the higher rate of profit as estimated.

The assessee carrying on business at Chettipalem in the State of Telangana purchased paddy from an unregistered dealer of Bihar. The said paddy reached at Chettipalem by train in railway wagons. When the paddy was off loaded from the railway wagons and loaded on to the lorries, the Assessing Authority intercepted the same and threatened to detain the goods on the ground that the goods were not accompanied by advance way bills mandated under rule 55(2) of the Telanagana VAT Rules, 2005. Thereupon the assessee paid tax at the rate of 5 per cent on the value of the goods as demanded by the Assessing Authority in order to avoid the risk of the goods getting detained.

Thereafter the Assessing Authority issued on the assessee a show-cause notice for imposition of penalty at the rate of 100 per cent under section 45(7)(a) of the Telangana VAT Act, 2005.

Against the action of the Assessing Authority, the assessee filed a writ petition and raised three contentions before the High Court, namely, (1) when the goods were imported from outside the State through railway wagons, the goods needed not be accompanied by advance way bills, since railway wagons did not come within the purview of the definition of goods vehicle under section 2(17) of the Telangana VAT Act, (2) the power of detention could be exercised by the Assessing Authority only at check posts and the railway lines or stations could not be construed as check posts, and (3) without an order of assessment, there could not be a levy and collection of tax.

The assessee-firm and its partners were assessed for the assessment years 1958-59, 1960-61 to 1962-63. The assessments of the firm were made on the slab rates prescribed under the respective Finance Acts applicable to registered firms, while the individual assessments of the partners were made in the status of non-resident at the maximum rates of taxes on their respective share income.

Later, the ITO sought to rectify the mistakes in those assessments inasmuch as the firm had not been charged at the maximum rates of income tax under section 17 of the 1922 Act. The assessee-firm objected to reopening of the assessments, but the ITO assessed the firm by applying the provisions of section 17(1) of the 1922 Act.

On writ, the High Court took the view that the original assessments were prima facie in accordance with the law and in any case as there was no obvious or patent mistake in those assessment orders, the ITO was incompetent to pass the impugned orders.

On appeal before the Supreme Court :

The assessee produced confectionery items and packed same in covers, which contained assessee's name, i.e., V.R.S. Confectionery, Rasipuram.

The Commissioner, on an application filed by assessee seeking clarification as regards the rate of tax for the confectionery items produced by it, clarified that the confectionery items produced by the assessee, which were branded, but the brand name was not registered, were taxable at 12 per cent under the residuary Entry No. 40 of Part D of the First Schedule of the Act.

The Assessing Authority, while framing the assessment of the assessee for the assessment year 2004-05, following the aforesaid clarification issued by the Commissioner, held that the confectionery items produced by the assessee and packed in covers containing the name of assessee were branded taxable at higher rate of 12 per cent under the residuary Entry No. 40 of Part D of the First Schedule of the Act.

On writ:

The assessee was carrying on the business of sale and purchase of lottery tickets on commission basis. A search was conducted at premises of the assessee during the course of which cash book, ledger and vouchers were seized. The assessee made a surrender under section 132(4) of Rs. 1,00,000 each for the assessment years 1993-94 and 1994-95. Thereafter, he filed the return of income for the assessment years 1989-90, 1991-92 to 1994-95. In the return filed for the assessment year 1993-94, the assessee declared an income of Rs. 1,35,000 which included an amount of Rs. 1,00,000 surrendered at the time of search. The Assessing Officer issued notice to the assessee under section 143(2) to disclose the basis on which he had estimated his income at Rs. 35,000, to furnish the statement indicating the total turnover, gross profit, gross expenses and net profit of the business. The assessee stated that the income of Rs. 35,000 was given out on estimate basis because the books of account were not available.

The Assessing Officer held that the seized books of account were not correct and complete. Accordingly, he invoked section 145(2) and assessed the income of the assessee on estimate basis at Rs. 10,48,000 by applying the gross profit rate of 55 per cent. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) granted part relief to the assessee to some extent. On second appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order of the Assessing Officer. However, the Tribunal directed the Assessing Officer to work out the income of the assessee by applying the gross profit rate of 27 per cent.

In appeal to the High Court, the assessee contended that the Assessing Officer and the Tribunal committed a serious error by invoking section 145 for assessing his income on estimate basis by taking into consideration gross profit at 27 per cent of the return ignoring the fact that he had regularly filed the returns and maintained the books of account etc.

The assessee had shown yield of paddy husk at 18.95 per cent and 10.95 per cent thereof towards consumption in its driers. The Assessing Officer referring to other rice millers determined total yield of husk at 20 per cent of paddy milled and 10 per cent thereof was allowed as having been consumed in the drier. As assessee had not shown sales of paddy husk in weight but by truck-load or tractor/trolley loads holding that it was not verifiable as to how much husk had been sold, the Assessing Officer proceeded to calculate the total sale price at the rate of Rs. 31 per quintal, allowance was given for transportation charges at rate of Rs. 10 per quintal. Therefore, sale price was determined at the rate of Rs. 21 per quintal at Rs. 5,48,730. The assessee had shown the sale of paddy husk at Rs. 83,055 only. Addition was thus made by the Assessing Officer at Rs. 4,65,675. On appeal, the assessee’s plea was that there were eight driers in which more than 50 per cent of the paddy husk was consumed. Sale bills were also produced so as to prove that paddy husk had been sold either by cart or truck loads, and not by actual weight. Appellate authority while upholding estimate of yield at 20 per cent accepted the claim of consumption of paddy husk and reduced the price from Rs. 21 to Rs. 16 per quintal as calculated by Assessing Officer. Consequently, the addition was reduced to Rs. 1,25,984.

On appeal by both the assessee and the revenue, the revenue contended that the sale price shown by the assessee was not verifiable and the calculation made by the Assessing Officer was appropriate. The assessee contended in the earlier years assessee had shown similar results which were accepted and since there was no defect in account books, it was not appropriate to simply raise presumption and to calculate the sale price at an assumed rate, and if the Assessing Officer developed any suspicion against the sale price, the proper course was to make an enquiry from the buyers. Therefore, the addition was unwarranted.

The assessee claimed to have received interest at the rate of 18 per cent from its various customers against the pawned jewellery. The Assessing Officer, however, on the basis of seized material recovered during search, which was conducted at premises of assessee, and following the order for the assessment year 1994-95 held that interest was received by the assessee at 24 per cent. The Assessing Officer, accordingly, enhanced the income by charging the interest at 24 per cent as against 18 per cent interest shown by the assessee. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) directed to apply interest of 21 per cent against the 24 per cent interest charged by the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

■

The assessee was a builder involved in development of various projects.

■

The Assessing Officer rejected the books of account of the assessee under section 145(3) and estimated income of the assessee at the rate of 10 per cent at Rs. 54.02 lakhs.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order passed by the Assessing Officer.

■

On the assessee’s appeal to the Tribunal:

During the assessment years 2001-02 to 2005-06, the assessee, a public sector undertaking, had deposited tax on the inter-State sale of tractors at the rate of 2 per cent, whereas it was required to pay tax at the rate of 4 per cent.

The Assessing Authority demanded additional tax at the rate of 2 per cent and also levied interest under section 9(2) of the Central Sales Tax Act read with section 25(5) of the Haryana General Sales Tax Act upon the assessee.

Both the First Appellate Authority and the Tribunal upheld the levy of interest.

On reference:

The assessee, was an individual carrying on business of plying, leasing and hiring of goods carriages. He had claimed the benefit of section 44AE and computed income from ten heavy goods vehicle on a presumptive rate.

The Assessing Officer on verification of the records found that the assessee had more than ten vehicles owned by him during the relevant previous year and held that fact that one vehicle was under repair was not a point to be considered while applying the presumptive rate provided under section 44AE and, the assessee was not entitled for the benefit of section 44AE.

The decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor (supra) was explained by the Apex Court itself in the case of Dr. Balbir Singh v. Municipal Corpn. of Delhi [1985] 152 ITR 388/ 20 Taxman 56 wherein it was held that the standard rent was the upper limit which could not be exceeded but where the actual rent received was reasonable but less than the standard rent, it was the actual rent which was assess- able. Where the actual rent was much more than the standard rent, then the ALV could not exceed the standard rent. In order to dilute the effect of the above judgment, section 23 was amended to the effect that where the actual rent was in excess of the rent determined under clause (a ), the actual rent would be assessable under section 23. Therefore, notional interest on the security deposit could not be taken into consideration for determining the ALV under section 23. The actual rent received by the assessee might be more or less than the standard rent and, therefore, the same also could not be the sale criterion for determining the ALV. Actual rent would be assessed only where it is in excess of the standard rent determined under clause (a) of section 23(1). In the instant case, neither of the lower authorities had made any exercise for determi-ning the standard rent. It was also not clear whether the provisions of Rent Control Legislation were applicable to the property in dispute. If the property was not the subject-matter of Rent Control Legislation, then the ALV could be determined on the basis of comparable cases. If the property was found to be governed by Rent Control Legislation, then ALV could be determined in accordance with the guidelines mentioned above. [Para 5]

Act, for determination of standard rent. The question, in the instant case, however, was that whether the Controller having fixed the standard rent in respect of the property-in-question in 1971, any revision thereof was warranted in the facts and circumstances of the case as per the relevant provisions of the 1958 Act as held by the Assessing Officer and whether such revision made by him was in accordance with the principles of valuation laid down in the 1958 Act. [Para 25] In the instant case, the property-in-question was a residential premises and the same having been let out by the assessee after 2-6-1944 (i.e. in the assessment year 1993-94) and no rent thereof having been filed under the Delhi & Ajmer-Merwar Rent Control Act, 1947 or the Delhi & Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, the determination of standard rent was required to be done by applying the provisions of sub-clause (2)(b ) of clause (A) of sub-section (1) of section 6 of the 1958 Act. It stipulates that the standard rent in case of the properties like the one in the instant case would be the rent calculated on the basis of 10 per cent per annum of the aggregate amount of the actual cost of construction and the market price of the land comprised in the premises on the date of the commencement of the construction. In the instant case, the land was purchased and construction of building thereon was done by the previous owner prior to 1971 and, thus, the standard rent of the said property fixed in 1971 could be taken as determined by the Controller taking into consideration the actual cost of construction incurred by the previous owner as well as the market price of the land comprised in the premises on the date of the commencement of the construction. At the relevant time, the rate to be applied to such cost for determining the standard rent was 7.5 per cent which had been, subsequently, increased with effect from 1-12-1988 to 10 per cent and the Controller, thus, would have applied the said rate of 7.5 per cent to such cost for determining the standard rent of the property in the year 1971. It was observed that the Assessing Officer, however, adopted a value of Rs. 37,61,541 paid by the assessee for the purchase of the said property from the previous owner as appearing in the accounts as on 1-6-1986 and added a further sum of Rs. 9,63,419 incurred on additions and alterations made to the property in the assessment year 1988-89 in order to apply the rate of 10 per cent to determine the standard rent. This method adopted by the Assessing Officer was not in accordance with the relevant provisions of section 6(2) of the 1958 Act as applicable to the instant case. The rate of 10 per cent applied by the Assessing Officer no doubt was correct but the cost of the property to the assessee as taken by him as the basis for applying the said rate was wrong because as per sub-clause (2)(b ) of clause (A) of section 6(1) of the 1958 Act, the aggregate amount of the actual cost of construction and the market price of the land comprised in the premises on the date of commencement of the construction was to be taken as the basis for applying the said rate in order to calculate the standard rent. What was relevant for this purpose, therefore, was the cost of construction actually incurred by previous owner or more so by the original owner as well as market price of the land on date of the commencement of the construction and not the cost of the property to the assessee. As already observed, the standard rent was determined by the Controller in the year 1971 and the land having been acquired by the previous owner prior to the year 1971 as well as the construction having been done by the said owner before 1971, the value to be taken as basis as per clause (A)( 2)(b ) of section 6(1) of the 1958 Act ought to have been already considered by the Controller while determining the standard rent in the year 1971 itself. This being so, it was not permissible as per the relevant provisions of section 6 of the 1958 Act to substitute the said base price with the cost of the property to the assessee in order to determine/revise the standard rent and the said cost, thus, was entirely irrelevant in the context of determining the standard rent of the property. [Para 27]

The rate of 40 per cent as specified in section 44AC, could not be applied to the case of L-14 licences in the light of the exception created in sub section (2) of the said section. After section 44AC was omitted, the provisions were incorporated to the same effect in section 206C. Goods received by the retail vends were in the nature of second sale from the L-13 licensee. There was no evidence on record to show that the L-14 licensee received any stock directly from the distillery. Though the assessee had maintained a combined trading and profit and loss account, that would not alter the character of the transaction. Purchases & sales were declared under three different licences. Therefore, the case of the L-14 licensee was covered under section 44AC(2) and the rate of 40 per cent was not required to be made applicable to the case of L-14 licensee. The provisions of sections 215 and 217(1)(a ) operate in different fields. Section 215 will be applicable where the assessee have filed their own estimates of advance tax including revised estimates which have been found to be false. Section 217(1)(a) operates in cases where assessees have failed to file a statement of advance tax. However, there is ambiguity in the Act. An assessee hitherto assessed is required to furnish a statement of advance tax under section 209A(1)(a) on the basis of the last assessed income or self-assessment tax paid thereafter. The ITO is also empowered under section 210 to raise advance tax demand on the basis of the last assessed income or self-assessment tax paid subsequently in the case of an assessee hitherto assessed. If the assessee has filed a statement of advance tax suo motu under section 209A(1)(a), then the action of the ITO in demanding advance tax under section 210 will be only a duplication of the demand and will, therefore, be infructuous. Similarly, if the ITO has demanded advance tax under section 210, then filing of the statement of advance tax by the assessee will also be a duplication and infructuous. If both the sections operate simultaneously, then it will tend to ambiguity. Therefore, only one of the provisions will operate at a time. In the instant case, since the ITO raised the demand under section 210, section 209A(1)(a) will not operate and, hence, no interest under section 217(1)(a ) would be leviable. Since the assessee filed its own estimate under section 212(1) as a result of the order under section 210, interest under section 215 was leviable. The interest levied under section 117(1)(a ) was, therefore, cancelled.

Before the Tribunal, by an application the assessee referred a comparable case of another dealer who was also on assessee, whose disclosure of 2 per cent was accepted. The Tribunal mentioned that most of the sales were ‘invoice sales’, which meant outstation sales, and the inference was that such sales usually carried a larger margin of profit than local sales. No attempt also appeared to have been made at any time before the Tribunal to split up the turnover of the business on commission basis and the turnover on own account so that different rates might be applied to such turnover. In these circumstances, the question as to the consideration of comparable case mentioned by the assessee did not really arise nor did the question regarding the splitting up of the turnover arise out of the order of the Tribunal.

In any event, it was well settled that, once a proviso to section 13 of the Act 1922 applied, it was for the ITO to determine fairly and not arbitrarily the basis on which the income will be estimated. In estimating the income the conditions of trade obtaining and the average margin of profit in the particular line of business are to be borne in mind. It was clear that these factors in the present case have been kept in view and, therefore, it was not possible to say that the estimate of income was arbitrary or capricious to justify holding that some error of law had been committed by the Tribunal in confirming the flat rate of 5 per cent applied by the departmental authorities. It was again well settled that an estimate can be made by applying a flat rate and, so long as the ITO had exercised his judgment reasonably and not arbitrarily or capriciously, the finding given by him will be one of fact and not of law.

For the reasons given above the application of the flat rate of 5 percent was justified and the income-tax authorities were not liable to split up the total estimated turnover of Rs. 1,50,000 into turnover of business on commission and turnover of business on own account and applied a lower rate of turnover from business on commission.

Two questions were considered by the Division Bench of the High Court in Ranchi Club Ltd. v. CIT [1996] 217 ITR 72/ 85 Taxman 201 (Pat.). Firstly, whether interest under sections 234A and 234B can be levied on the tax payable on the returned income or tax payable on the assessed income and secondly, whether in absence of any specific order of the assessing authority, interest could be charged and recovered from the assessee. The Division Bench firstly held that in absence of any specific order of the assessing authority charging interest, no interest could be recovered from the assessee. Secondly, it was held that interest is leviable on the tax on the total income as declared in the return and not on the income as determined by the assessing authority. It was, therefore, clear that the question referred in the instant case was decided by the Division Bench in the case of Ranchi Club Ltd. (supra) and the said judgment was affirmed by the Supreme Court (See Annex). It may be noted that the Supreme Court, after hearing the parties, dismissed the appeal. Therefore, it was not a case where special leave petition was summarily dismissed by the Supreme Court, rather civil appeal was heard on merit and thereafter it was dismissed holding that the appeal had no merit.

It is well-settled principle of law that when a special leave petition is summarily dismissed under article 136 of the Constitution, such dismissal does not lay down any law; rather it shall be deemed that the Supreme Court has simply held that it is not a fit case where special leave petition should be granted. The same principle will not apply in a case where civil appeal is dismissed by the Supreme Court holding that the appeal has no merit. When once civil appeal is dismissed after hearing the parties by the Supreme Court holding that the appeal has no merit, then such order becomes one which attracts article 141 of the Constitution, which provides that the law declared by the Supreme Court shall be binding on all the Courts within the territory of India.

Having regard to the law laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of V.M. Salgaocar & Bros. (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2000] 243 ITR 383/110 Taxman 67, the questions referred to the Full Bench had been completely answered by the Division Bench of the High Court in the assessee's case, and the same had been affirmed in civil appeal by the Supreme Court. Hence, there was no question of going any further and taking a different view in the matter.

Further from examining the various provisions, it is manifest that assessment made under section 143 includes reassessment as well. An assessment made in pursuance of a notice under section 148 is a regular assessment under section 143 or section 144. Section 140A provides that any admitted tax paid in pursuance of this section shall be deemed to have been paid towards a regular assessment under section 143 or 144. Accordingly, any assessment made for the first time by resort to section 147 would also be a regular assessment for the purpose of section 143.

From reading of provisions of sections 234A and 234B along with Explanation, it is clear that tax on the total income as determined under section 143(1) or on regular assessment shall be deemed to be tax on total income as declared in the return for the purpose of computing the interest payable under section 140A. Also, the additional liability to pay interest arises only on account of delayed filing of return or non-filing of return and also on account of delayed or non-payment of advance tax. According to the CBDT Circular No. 549, dated 31-10-1989, if the returned income is increased either as a result of adjustment made under the first proviso to section 143(1)(a) or as a result of regular assessment under section 143(3) so that the advance tax paid becomes less than 90 per cent of the tax on the total income determined under section 143(1)(a) or on a regular assessment, interest under section 234A will also be increased on the basis of the tax on total income determined under section 143(1)(c) or on regular assessment.

Explanation 4 to section 234A fully clarifies the position by explaining that tax on the total income as determined under sub-section (1) of section 143 or on regular assessment shall be deemed to be the tax on total income as declared in the return for the purpose of computing the interest payable under section 140A.

The wording of section 66 (2) of the 1922 Act does not lay on the assessee the duty of formulating any questions of law, although it is open to him to do so for the benefit of the Commissioner. It ought to be sufficient for him to indicate that the order of the Commissioner upholding the assessment gives rise to questions of law and that he wants him to state his case for the decision of this Court. The law casts on the Commissioner the duty of drawing up a statement of the case. No rules or departmental instructions had been brought by the Commissioner, making it obligatory on the assessee to specify or even to formulate the questions of law arising out of the Commissioners order at the time when he moved the Commissioner to state his case under section 66. It thus follows that the duty of stating the case for the decision of the High Court in such a clear manner as to enable it to determine the question raised thereby rests on the Commissioner and not on the assessee. After the Commissioner refused to state his case the law vests in the assessee the right to move this court for compelling the Commissioner to make reference on the ground that his case involves questions of law, and this Court on being satisfied that the Commissioners view that no questions of law are involved is not correct, can issue directions to him to state the case. It is sufficient for the purposes of the reference if the questions set forth in the petition to this Court arise out of the Commissioners order passed under section 31 or section 32 of the 1922 Act.

Therefore an assessee is entitled to move the High Court for a direction to the Commissioner to refer questions of law raised by him in his petition to the High Court even though they may not have been raised before him in the course of the proceedings under section 66(2) provided that they are questions of law arising out of the Commissioners order passed in appeal.

Under section 22 and section 23(4) of the 1922 Act it is the duty of the assessee to supply the materials of his assessment. If he fails to supply or having supplied fails, to substantiate the same under section 23 (3) the ITO has still to assess the total income of the assessee to the best of his judgment as contemplated by section 23 (4) of the 1922 Act.

The assessee’s accounts being unclosed he was unable to supply the full material, much less to substantiate the same. Realizing this difficulty the assessee in his oral statement admitted that he had nothing to say if some fair percentage was adopted to find out his income. On the facts ascertained by the Assistant Commissioner in his enquiry assessee had no reason to think that the rate of 2 per cent was unreasonable and the Commissioner also had confirmed the same. The reasonableness or otherwise of the rate applied could not be a question of law which would be agitated. Had the assessee disputed in his statement the authority of the Income tax Department of adopt a flat rate, then question of law might have arisen for consideration as to whether in the absence of other reliable data as to income of an assessee from a certain source an ITO is justified in making an assessment based on a formula deduced by taking a certain percentage of the gross turn over, as representing a fair margin of profit. But on the admission made by the assessee in this behalf that question did not arise. Therefore, it followed that it was not open to him to argue merely the question of the unreasonableness of the extent of the percentage adopted.

As for as second item was concerned, it was an admitted fact that even though the liability for adat charges was incurred during the Samvat year 1978-79, the same had not been paid to the Adatya before the close of the year. The Commissioner was, therefore, right in disallowing this item as it was not expenditure incurred for earning the profits of the account year within the meaning of section 10(ix), or section 11(2) of the 1922 Act. No doubt it could be termed a liability incurred so long it was not satisfied. But it appeared the Income tax Act for obvious reasons did not take into account mere monitary obligation or liabilities incurred. The Commissioner was, therefore, right in refusing to allow the deduction. The sum paid on account of interest to others for the business would certainly be debitable against the gross income of the business under section 11(2). The Commissioner’s opinion showed that might have allowed those deductions had the assessee furnished the necessary details and shown that the payment made was before the end of the account year.

A part of this amount was paid after the assessment order was made, i.e., after the accounts were examined. Thus the Commissioner entertained doubts about the correctness of the debit and thought fit to disallow it.

The union board rate is only imposed on persons who are owners or occupiers or owners and occupiers of buildings within the union, but, in arriving at the amount to be assessed on any such person, it is provided by section 38(1) of the 1919 Act that the assessment is to be according "to the circumstances within the union and property within the union, if any", of the assessee, with a maximum limit of Rs. 84 in any one year in the case of any assessee. Under section 39 of the 1919 Act the assessment for the imposition of the rate is to be made in accordance with rules prescribed under section 101 of the 1919 Act.

In order to determine under rule 3, "the total assessable income of the person concerned, i.e., the income which he derives from business conducted, or from buildings or other property held, within the union", the board have before them the information prepared under rule 2, which shows the buildings occupied or owned in the union, permanently or temporarily, and also "their trade, business, etc., within the union, and the estimated annual income which they derive from buildings or other property or business within the union."

In the absence of the necessary powers and machinery, which are not provided by the Act, the estimate of the annual income from business can only proceed on a rough guess, which is in no way comparable with the ascertainment of profits and gains under the 1922 Act, and the inclusion of this element of business income as part of the "circumstances" of the assessee with a view to the imposition of the union rate did not fall within sub-section (4) of section 10 of the 1922 Act. It was conceded that the union rate was not "levied on the profits or gains," which clearly implies an ascertainment of such profits and gains, and the words "assessed on the basis of any such profits or gains" in the later part of the sub-section must also be so limited. No such ascertainment of the profits and gains of the business could be undertaken for the purposes of the union rate.

The decision of the Appellate Tribunal, the question of law referred, and the decision of the High Court, proceed on the footing that the Rs. 84 solely related to the premises occupied for the purpose of the Naihati business, and, it being admitted that the union rate was a local rate, the amount was allowable deduction in computing profits of business, under section 10 of the 1922 Act. However, in any case where the union rate is not wholly referable to premises occupied for the purpose of a business or businesses, the assessee, on establishing the portion of the rate which is so referable, would be entitled to deduct such portion under section 10(2)(ix) of the 1922 Act.

The appeal was dismissed.

In the instant case the assessee did not allege that he derived no income at all from any contracts, nor did the assessment proceed definitely on the ground that the accounts were unreliable. The Assistant Commissioner adopted a standard rate for the assessment merely because no separate accounts were available for the accounting year. This was apparently due to the manner in which the accounting were kept. As the assessee failed to produce correct and complete accounts for the accounting year, it was open to the Income-tax Officer to make an assessment to the best of his judgment: vide section 23, read with section 11, of the 1922 Act. The Assistant Commissioner, however, gave no reasons for adopting what he called the usual rate of 10 per cent for the purposes of the assessment, and it was not known how that rate was arrived at. In the circumstances of the case, the point of law emerged for decision was whether in the case of a contract spread over a number of years when accounts for the year under assessment could not be separated, the ITO was legally justified in assessing profits at a flat rate without informing the assessee of the information or evidence on which the rate was based and without giving him any opportunity to produce evidence in rebuttal.

Accordingly, the petition was accepted and the Commissioner was directed to state the case and refer the point of law to the High Court for decision.
